name: Language & Literature
tagline: First the letters, then the words, then the worlds.

nodes.title: The Alphabet
nodes.goal: Know every letter by sight and sound.

lesson_media.alt: Three wooden blocks show A, B and C above an apple, a blue ball and a cat.
lesson_media.caption: The basic English alphabet has 26 letters, each with an uppercase and lowercase form. A letter has a name and can represent different sounds in different words.

lesson_media.title: Meet the 26 letters
lesson_media.instructions: Choose a letter or move one step at a time. Compare its uppercase and lowercase forms and explore one common word that begins with it. Use Read aloud to hear the current letter and word.

nodes.kid_text: The English alphabet is a little parade of 26 letters, and each one has a name. When you sing "A, B, C, D..." you are saying those names in order. Letters help us write the sounds in words, but the same letter can sound different in different words. Find the letter that starts your name, or the name of someone you know, and say hello!

quiz.prompt: Which one is a letter?
choices: B
quiz.answer: B
quiz.say: Which one of these is a letter? Is it B, or the number five, or a picture of a dog?
quiz.explain: Yes! B is a letter, and letters build words.

quiz.prompt: Sing it! A, B, C, then what?
choices: D
M
Z
quiz.answer: D
quiz.say: Let's sing together. A, B, C... which letter comes next? Is it D, M, or Z?
quiz.explain: D comes right after C in the alphabet parade.

quiz.prompt: Which letter starts 🍎 apple?
choices: A
P
S
quiz.answer: A
quiz.say: Apple! Which letter does apple start with? Is it A, P, or S?
quiz.explain: Apple starts with A, the first letter in the English alphabet. The letter A can represent other sounds in other words too.

quiz.prompt: Which letter comes after M?
choices: N
P
A
quiz.answer: N
quiz.say: Let's say them together. K, L, M... which letter comes next? Is it N, P, or A?
quiz.explain: N comes right after M in the alphabet parade.

quiz.prompt: Which one is a letter? 🎈
choices: K
quiz.answer: K
quiz.say: Which one of these is a letter? The number seven, a balloon, or K?
quiz.explain: K is a letter. Numbers and pictures are not letters.

quiz.prompt: Which letter is last of all?
choices: G
Z
B
quiz.answer: Z
quiz.say: The alphabet song ends with one special letter. Is it G, Z, or B?
quiz.explain: Z is the very last letter, right at the end of the song.

quiz.prompt: Which letter starts 🐝 bee?
choices: E
D
B
quiz.answer: B
quiz.say: Bee! Which letter does bee start with? Is it E, D, or B?
quiz.explain: Bee begins with the /b/ sound. The letter B represents that sound at the start of this word.

nodes.title: Letter Sounds
nodes.goal: Match letters to the sounds they make.
nodes.kid_text: Every letter makes a sound, like a tiny voice hiding inside it. The letter S hisses like a snake, "sss," and the letter B bounces its lips together, "buh." When you press the sounds together — "b" and "buh"... you can even hear the start of "ball!" Try making the sound your favorite letter says.

quiz.prompt: Which letter hisses sss? 🐍
choices: S
M
T
quiz.answer: S
quiz.say: A snake hisses ssss. Which letter makes that sound? Is it S, M, or T?
quiz.explain: Yes! S says sss, just like a snake.

quiz.prompt: Which letter says mmm? 😋
choices: M
B
F
quiz.answer: M
quiz.say: Listen: mmm, like yummy food. Which letter makes that sound? Is it M, B, or F?
quiz.explain: M says mmm, with your lips pressed together.

quiz.prompt: What sound starts 🐶 dog?
choices: duh
buh
sss
quiz.answer: duh
quiz.say: Dog. Listen to the very first sound: d-d-dog. Is it duh, buh, or sss?
quiz.explain: Dog starts with duh, the sound the letter D makes.

quiz.prompt: Which letter buzzes zzz? 🐝
choices: Z
P
L
quiz.answer: Z
quiz.say: A bee buzzes zzzz. Which letter makes that sound? Is it Z, P, or L?
quiz.explain: Z says zzz, just like a busy little bee.

quiz.prompt: What sound starts 🐈 cat?
choices: tuh
kuh
fff
quiz.answer: kuh
quiz.say: Cat. Listen to the very first sound: c-c-cat. Is it tuh, kuh, or fff?
quiz.explain: Cat starts with kuh, the sound the letter C makes.

quiz.prompt: Which letter says fff? 🍃
choices: N
D
F
quiz.answer: F
quiz.say: Listen: fff, like wind in the leaves. Which letter makes that sound? N, D, or F?
quiz.explain: F says fff, with your top teeth on your lip.

quiz.prompt: What sound starts 🎈 balloon?
choices: buh
lll
sss
quiz.answer: buh
quiz.say: Balloon. Listen to the beginning: b-b-balloon. Is it buh, lll, or sss?
quiz.explain: Balloon starts with buh, the sound the letter B makes.

lesson_media.alt: The written word cat is separated into C, A and T, matched to three speech sounds, then blended back into the spoken word cat.
lesson_media.caption: Phonics links graphemes with phonemes and blends the phonemes in sequence. English mappings are useful but not perfectly one-to-one: the same letter can represent different sounds.

nodes.title: Rhymes and Songs
nodes.goal: Hear rhythm and rhyme in language.
nodes.kid_text: Some words sound like they hold hands at the end: cat and hat, star and car. When words rhyme, they make a little bounce your ears love, like a song. Say "twinkle, twinkle" and clap along — can you feel the beat tap-tapping? Now find a word that rhymes with "sun"!

quiz.prompt: Which word rhymes with cat? 🐱
choices: hat
dog
cup
quiz.answer: hat
quiz.say: Cat. Which word rhymes with cat? Is it hat, dog, or cup?
quiz.explain: Cat and hat rhyme because they end with the same sound.

quiz.prompt: Which word rhymes with sun? ☀️
choices: run
tree
milk
quiz.answer: run
quiz.say: Sun. Which word sounds like sun at the end? Is it run, tree, or milk?
quiz.explain: Sun and run rhyme, and your ears can feel the little bounce.

quiz.prompt: Do star and car rhyme? ⭐🚗
choices: yes
no
quiz.answer: yes
quiz.say: Listen carefully: star, car. Do those two words rhyme? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! Star and car both finish with the same aaar sound.

quiz.prompt: Which word rhymes with bee? 🐝
choices: tree
book
fish
quiz.answer: tree
quiz.say: Bee. Which word rhymes with bee? Is it tree, book, or fish?
quiz.explain: Bee and tree rhyme, because they end the very same way.

quiz.prompt: Which word rhymes with cake? 🎂
choices: moon
lake
sock
quiz.answer: lake
quiz.say: Cake. Which word sounds like cake at the end? Moon, lake, or sock?
quiz.explain: Cake and lake rhyme with a happy little bounce.

quiz.prompt: Do moon and spoon rhyme? 🌙🥄
choices: no
yes
quiz.answer: yes
quiz.say: Listen carefully: moon, spoon. Do those two words rhyme? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! Moon and spoon both finish with the same oooon sound.

quiz.prompt: Which word rhymes with bed? 🛏️
choices: cup
fan
red
quiz.answer: red
quiz.say: Bed. Which word rhymes with bed? Is it cup, fan, or red?
quiz.explain: Bed and red rhyme, and your ears can feel the match.

lesson_media.alt: Cat, hat and sun are split into beginning and ending sound groups; cat and hat share the ending at while four beat marks show a steady pulse.
lesson_media.caption: A rhyme repeats a final stressed vowel and following sounds, as cat and hat do. Rhythm is a separate pattern of beats, so a poem can have rhythm without every line rhyming.

nodes.title: Story Time
nodes.goal: Follow a story: who, where, what happened.
nodes.kid_text: Every story tells you three big things: who it is about, where they are, and what happened to them. When you hear a story, be a detective — listen for the who (maybe a little bear), the where (maybe a deep forest), and the what (maybe he got lost). When it ends, try telling me who was in it. You just caught the whole story!

quiz.prompt: Who was the story about? 📖
choices: bear
fish
car
quiz.answer: bear
quiz.say: Here is a tiny story. A little bear got lost in the deep woods. Who was the story about? A bear, a fish, or a car?
quiz.explain: The bear is the who, the one the story is all about.

quiz.prompt: Where was the little bear? 📖
choices: woods
beach
moon
quiz.answer: woods
quiz.say: The little bear got lost in the deep woods. Where was he? In the woods, at the beach, or on the moon?
quiz.explain: The woods is the where, the place the story happens.

quiz.prompt: What happened to the bear?
choices: lost
slept
flew
quiz.answer: lost
quiz.say: The little bear walked and walked and could not find his way home. What happened to him? He got lost, he slept, or he flew?
quiz.explain: He got lost, and that is the what, the thing that happened.

quiz.prompt: Who lost her hat? 📖
choices: duck
bear
boy
quiz.answer: duck
quiz.say: Here is a tiny story. A little duck lost her hat down at the pond. Who lost her hat? A duck, a bear, or a boy?
quiz.explain: The duck is the who, the one the story is all about.

quiz.prompt: Where was the little duck? 📖
choices: zoo
pond
farm
quiz.answer: pond
quiz.say: The little duck was splashing at the pond. Where was she? At the zoo, the pond, or the farm?
quiz.explain: The pond is the where, the place the story happens.

quiz.prompt: The duck lost her ... ? 🦆
choices: cup
ball
hat
quiz.answer: hat
quiz.say: The little duck was wearing something on her head, and the wind blew it away. What did she lose? A cup, a ball, or her hat?
quiz.explain: She lost her hat, and that is the what, the thing that happened.

quiz.prompt: Who hid under the bed? 🛏️
choices: cat
mouse
robin
quiz.answer: mouse
quiz.say: Here is a new story. A tiny mouse hid under the bed. Who hid? A cat, a mouse, or a robin?
quiz.explain: The mouse hid, so the mouse is the who in this story.

lesson_media.alt: A story map follows Mina in a garden from a missing key through searching under leaves to finding the key, with who and where identified first.
lesson_media.caption: Listeners can reconstruct a story by tracking its character and setting, then arranging events causally: Mina loses a key, searches, and finds it under the leaves.

nodes.title: Talking and Listening
nodes.goal: Take turns, ask questions, tell about your day.
nodes.kid_text: Talking is like playing catch: one person throws words, then the other person catches and throws back. When someone else is talking, you listen and wait, and then it's your turn. If you want to know something, you can ask a question, like "Why is the sky blue?" Tell me one happy thing that happened to you today — I'll listen!

quiz.prompt: Someone is talking. What do you do? 🗣️
choices: listen
shout
run
quiz.answer: listen
quiz.say: Someone else is talking to you right now. What should you do? Listen, shout, or run away?
quiz.explain: We listen quietly, and then it is our turn to talk.

quiz.prompt: Which one is a question?
choices: Why?
Hello
Bye
quiz.answer: Why?
quiz.say: Which one of these is a question? Why? Or hello. Or bye.
quiz.explain: Why is a question, because it asks somebody to tell you something.

quiz.prompt: Two people talk at once. Good? 🗣️🗣️
choices: yes
no
quiz.answer: no
quiz.say: If two people talk at exactly the same time, can they hear each other? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: No, so we take turns, like throwing a ball back and forth.

quiz.prompt: Which one asks a question?
choices: Please
Where?
Yum
quiz.answer: Where?
quiz.say: Which one of these asks a question? Please. Or where? Or yum.
quiz.explain: Where is a question, because it asks somebody to tell you something.

quiz.prompt: A friend is talking. Do you butt in? 🗣️
choices: no
yes
quiz.answer: no
quiz.say: Your friend is still talking. Should you butt in and talk over them? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: No, we wait for our turn, like passing a ball back and forth.

quiz.prompt: Someone asks your name. You should… 🙂
choices: ignore
answer
shout
quiz.answer: answer
quiz.say: Someone kindly asks what your name is. Should you ignore them, answer them, or shout?
quiz.explain: We answer kindly, and that keeps the talking going.

quiz.prompt: Should you look at the talker? 🗣️
choices: no
yes
quiz.answer: yes
quiz.say: When someone is talking to you, should you look at them? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: Yes, looking at them shows your ears are listening too.

lesson_media.alt: Four linked stages form a conversation loop: one person asks, the other listens, answers the question, and checks whether the message was understood.
lesson_media.caption: Conversation is coordinated turn-taking. A relevant response depends on listening to the previous turn, and a check or follow-up question repairs misunderstandings.

nodes.title: Learning to Read
nodes.goal: Read and understand whole sentences and short books.

lesson_media.alt: An open book shows the words 'THE CAT SAT.' beside a drawing of an orange cat while a finger points along the sentence.
lesson_media.caption: Readers connect speech sounds to written words, then use the whole sentence to make meaning. English lines usually run from left to right; other writing systems may use other directions.

lesson_media.title: Build meaning from sounds
lesson_media.instructions: Follow one simple English sentence from individual sounds through blending, words and meaning. Move between phases or reset to the beginning; reading with another person or an accessibility support is valid too.

nodes.kid_text: Reading connects written words with language and ideas. You might follow print with a finger, read braille, listen while following the words, or read with help from a person or tool. For many English words, saying the sounds and blending them can reveal the word — "the cat sat." English lines usually run from left to right, while other writing systems may use other directions. However you access the words, a sentence can open a whole adventure!

quiz.prompt: The cat sat on the mat. Who sat?
choices: cat
mat
dog
quiz.answer: cat
quiz.say: Here is a sentence: The cat sat on the mat. Who sat down? Was it the cat, the mat, or a dog?
quiz.explain: The cat sat! You read a whole sentence and understood it.

quiz.prompt: Blend it: p - i - g
choices: pig
pug
big
quiz.answer: pig
quiz.say: Listen for the first sound in pan, the short i sound in sit, and the first sound in go. What word do they make — pig, pug, or big?
quiz.explain: Those three sounds blend into pig. Keeping them close together helps the word emerge.

quiz.prompt: In English, where does a line usually start? 📖
choices: left
right
middle
quiz.answer: left
quiz.say: When you read a line of English words, which side does it usually start on? The left, the right, or the middle?
quiz.explain: English lines usually begin on the left and continue to the right. Other writing systems can use other directions.

quiz.prompt: Blend it: c - a - t
choices: cot
bat
cat
quiz.answer: cat
quiz.say: Listen for the first sound in cup, the short a sound in map, and the first sound in top. What word do they make — cot, bat, or cat?
quiz.explain: Those three sounds blend into cat. Keeping them close together helps the word emerge.

quiz.prompt: Sam has a red hat. What color? 🎩
choices: Red
Blue
Green
quiz.answer: Red
quiz.say: Read with me: Sam has a red hat. What colour is the hat? Red, blue, or green?
quiz.explain: The words tell you the hat is red. You used the sentence to find the answer.

quiz.prompt: The dog is under the bed. Where? 🐕
choices: Under
Beside
On top
quiz.answer: Under
quiz.say: Here is a sentence: The dog is under the bed. Where is the dog? Under it, beside it, or on top of it?
quiz.explain: Under the bed! Every word in a sentence tells you something.

quiz.prompt: The bird can fly. Can it fly? 🐦
choices: no
yes
quiz.answer: yes
quiz.say: Read this with me: The bird can fly. So, can the bird fly? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! You read the sentence and knew exactly what it meant.

nodes.title: Spelling
nodes.goal: Spell everyday words correctly.
nodes.kid_text: Spelling means putting a word's letters in the right order so everyone can read it. Say the word slowly and listen for each sound, then write a letter for each one, left to right — "f-r-o-g" spells frog. Some tricky words you just have to remember, like a secret code. The more you practice, the more words become your friends.

quiz.prompt: Which one spells 🐸?
choices: frog
forg
frg
quiz.answer: frog
quiz.say: Which one spells frog? Is it f-r-o-g, or f-o-r-g, or f-r-g?
quiz.explain: Frog is f, r, o, g, one letter for each little sound.

quiz.prompt: Which one spells 🐱?
choices: cat
kat
cta
quiz.answer: cat
quiz.say: Which one spells cat? Is it c-a-t, or k-a-t, or c-t-a?
quiz.explain: Cat begins with the letter C, then a, then t.

quiz.prompt: Which one spells ☀️?
choices: sun
sn
son
quiz.answer: sun
quiz.say: Which one spells the sun up in the sky? Is it s-u-n, or s-n, or s-o-n?
quiz.explain: The sun in the sky is spelled s, u, n.

quiz.prompt: Which one spells 🐕?
choices: dog
dgo
dawg
quiz.answer: dog
quiz.say: Which one spells dog? Is it d-o-g, or d-g-o, or d-a-w-g?
quiz.explain: Dog is d, o, g, one letter for each little sound.

quiz.prompt: Which one spells 🏠?
choices: howse
house
hos
quiz.answer: house
quiz.say: Which one spells house? Is it h-o-w-s-e, or h-o-u-s-e, or h-o-s?
quiz.explain: House is h, o, u, s, e. That tricky u you just remember.

quiz.prompt: Which one spells 🌳?
choices: tre
teer
tree
quiz.answer: tree
quiz.say: Which one spells tree? Is it t-r-e, or t-e-e-r, or t-r-e-e?
quiz.explain: Tree needs two e's at the end: t, r, e, e.

quiz.prompt: Fill it in: b _ d 🛏️
choices: a
e
o
quiz.answer: e
quiz.say: The word is bed. Which letter belongs in the middle? A, e, or o?
quiz.explain: Bed is b, e, d, with a little e humming in the middle.

lesson_media.alt: The spoken word ship is segmented into three ordered phonemes, mapped to the graphemes SH, I and P, then checked against the complete written word.
lesson_media.caption: Segmenting speech helps select graphemes in order. Ship has three phonemes but four letters because the digraph SH represents one phoneme; English spellings still need visual or dictionary checks.

nodes.title: Word Collecting
nodes.goal: Grow a hoard of wonderful words.
nodes.kid_text: Words are like treasures, and you can collect them your whole life! Every time you meet a new word — like "gigantic," which means really, really big — you can pop it in your word hoard and use it later. The more words you keep, the better you can say exactly what you mean. What shiny new word did you catch today?

quiz.prompt: Gigantic means…
choices: huge
tiny
wet
quiz.answer: huge
quiz.say: Here is a big word: gigantic. Does it mean huge, tiny, or wet?
quiz.explain: Gigantic means really, really big, like an elephant.

quiz.prompt: Which word means very happy? 😄
choices: joyful
sleepy
angry
quiz.answer: joyful
quiz.say: Which word means very, very happy? Joyful, sleepy, or angry?
quiz.explain: Joyful means full of joy, with happiness bubbling right over.

quiz.prompt: Tiny means the same as…
choices: small
loud
fast
quiz.answer: small
quiz.say: Here is the word tiny. Which word means the same thing? Small, loud, or fast?
quiz.explain: Tiny and small mean the same thing. Some words are twins!

quiz.prompt: Freezing means very…
choices: cold
hot
wet
quiz.answer: cold
quiz.say: Here is a word: freezing. Does it mean cold, hot, or wet?
quiz.explain: Freezing means very, very cold, like ice and snow.

quiz.prompt: Which word means very tired? 😴
choices: brave
weary
kind
quiz.answer: weary
quiz.say: Which word means very, very tired? Brave, weary, or kind?
quiz.explain: Weary means so tired you just want to flop down and rest.

quiz.prompt: Minuscule means the same as…
choices: small
quick
huge
quiz.answer: small
quiz.say: Minuscule means the same as which word? Small, quick, or huge?
quiz.explain: Minuscule means very small indeed.

quiz.prompt: Which word means not loud?
choices: spicy
quiet
tall
quiz.answer: quiet
quiz.say: Which word means not loud at all? Spicy, quiet, or tall?
quiz.explain: Quiet is soft and hushed, like a little whisper.

lesson_media.alt: Three word choices climb an intensity scale from big through huge to enormous, then the strongest word is used in the sentence An enormous wave crossed the wall.
lesson_media.caption: Vocabulary adds distinctions, not just substitutes. Choosing enormous rather than big encodes greater scale, while context determines whether that stronger word is accurate.

nodes.title: Sentences
nodes.goal: Build complete sentences with capital letters and full stops.
nodes.kid_text: A sentence is a complete thought, dressed up with a capital letter at the front and a full stop at the end. The capital letter stands tall like a flag saying "we're starting here," and the full stop is a little dot that means "all done." "The dog ran fast." — see the big T and the dot? Try saying a whole thought, then imagine the capital and the stop.

quiz.prompt: What mark ends a sentence?
choices: B
quiz.say: What little mark do we put at the end of a sentence? A full stop dot, a comma, or the letter B?
quiz.explain: A full stop is a tiny dot that says the thought is all done.

quiz.prompt: Is 'The dog ran.' a whole sentence? 🐕
choices: yes
no
quiz.answer: yes
quiz.say: Listen: The dog ran. Is that a whole finished thought? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! It tells us who and what they did, so it is a sentence.

quiz.prompt: Which letter starts a sentence?
choices: big
tiny
quiz.answer: big
quiz.say: Every sentence begins with a capital, a letter standing up tall. Is that first letter big or tiny?
quiz.explain: Big! A capital letter tells us a brand new sentence is starting.

quiz.prompt: Is 'A big red' a whole sentence? 🤔
choices: yes
no
quiz.answer: no
quiz.say: Listen to this: a big red. Is that a whole finished thought? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: No, it stops too soon. A big red what? It needs more.

quiz.prompt: Where does the full stop go? ⚫
choices: start
end
middle
quiz.answer: end
quiz.say: A sentence has a little dot called a full stop. Does it go at the start, the end, or the middle?
quiz.explain: The full stop goes at the end and means the thought is done.

quiz.prompt: Is 'Fish swim.' a whole sentence? 🐟
choices: yes
no
quiz.answer: yes
quiz.say: Listen to this: Fish swim. Is that a whole finished thought? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! It tells us who and what they do, so it is a sentence.

lesson_media.alt: The sentence The dog ran fast is assembled from a capitalized subject, a predicate that completes the thought, and a full stop at the end.
lesson_media.caption: A written English sentence expresses a complete clause and marks its boundary. Here The dog is the subject, ran fast is the predicate, and capitalization plus punctuation show the limits.

nodes.title: Handwriting
nodes.goal: Write clearly and comfortably.
nodes.kid_text: Handwriting is drawing letters so neatly that anyone can read them. Hold your pencil gently, like a little bird you don't want to squeeze, and rest your other hand on the paper to keep it still. Make each letter sit on the line, not too big and not too tiny. Take your time — slow and tidy beats fast and messy every time.

quiz.prompt: How do you hold a pencil? ✏️
choices: gently
tight
fist
quiz.answer: gently
quiz.say: How should you hold your pencil? Gently, very tight, or squeezed in a fist?
quiz.explain: Hold it gently, like a little bird you do not want to squash.

quiz.prompt: Where should each letter sit? 📄
choices: line
air
edge
quiz.answer: line
quiz.say: When you write, where should each letter sit? On the line, up in the air, or off the edge?
quiz.explain: Letters sit neatly on the line so everyone can read them.

quiz.prompt: Which writing is easier to read? 🖊️
choices: neat
messy
quiz.answer: neat
quiz.say: If you want everybody to read your words, should your writing be neat or messy?
quiz.explain: Slow and neat beats fast and messy every single time.

quiz.prompt: What holds the paper still? 📄
choices: hand
foot
nose
quiz.answer: hand
quiz.say: While you write, what should hold the paper still? Your other hand, your foot, or your nose?
quiz.explain: Your other hand rests on the paper so it cannot wiggle away.

quiz.prompt: How big should your letters be? 📄
choices: giant
teeny
even
quiz.answer: even
quiz.say: Should your letters be giant, teeny, or all the same even size?
quiz.explain: Even letters, not too big and not too small, are easy to read.

quiz.prompt: Writing too fast makes it… 🏃
choices: neater
messy
bigger
quiz.answer: messy
quiz.say: If you scribble as fast as you can, does your writing come out neater, messy, or bigger?
quiz.explain: Rushing makes it messy, so slow down and take your time.

quiz.prompt: Is it okay to write slowly? ⏳
choices: no
yes
quiz.answer: yes
quiz.say: When you are making your letters, is it okay to go nice and slowly? Say yes or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! Slow hands make tidy letters that everyone can read.

lesson_media.alt: A handwriting sequence shows a relaxed grip, baseline and midline guides, the ordered strokes for a lowercase a, and a final check for size and spacing.
lesson_media.caption: Legibility comes from repeatable letter formation, alignment, spacing, and a comfortable grip. Checking the result matters more than writing quickly.

nodes.title: Great Children's Books
nodes.goal: Read classic stories and talk about them.
nodes.kid_text: Some stories are so wonderful that children have loved them for a hundred years — like fairy tales with brave heroes, hungry wolves, and magic beans. When you finish one, you can talk about it: which part was your favorite, and what would YOU have done? Sharing a story with someone makes it twice as fun. Pick a classic tale and let's talk about the ending!

quiz.prompt: Who huffed and puffed? 📖
choices: wolf
pig
bear
quiz.answer: wolf
quiz.say: In the Three Little Pigs, who huffed and puffed to blow the house down? The wolf, a pig, or a bear?
quiz.explain: The wolf huffed and puffed, but the brick house stayed standing!

quiz.prompt: Jack climbed up a… 📖
choices: beanstalk
ladder
tree
quiz.answer: beanstalk
quiz.say: In Jack and the Beanstalk, what did Jack climb up? A beanstalk, a ladder, or a tree?
quiz.explain: Jack climbed the magic beanstalk all the way up to the clouds.

quiz.prompt: After a story, what is fun to do? 📖
choices: talk
hide
nap
quiz.answer: talk
quiz.say: When you finish a lovely story, what is fun to do with someone? Talk about it, hide, or take a nap?
quiz.explain: Talking about a story with someone makes it twice as fun.

quiz.prompt: Who tasted the three bears' porridge? 🐻
choices: Jack
Goldilocks
Snow White
quiz.answer: Goldilocks
quiz.say: In the story of the three bears, who tasted their porridge? Jack, Goldilocks, or Snow White?
quiz.explain: Goldilocks tried all three bowls and liked the little one best.

quiz.prompt: Whose nose grew when he fibbed? 👃
choices: Pinocchio
Peter Pan
Bambi
quiz.answer: Pinocchio
quiz.say: In this famous tale, whose nose grew longer every time he fibbed? Pinocchio, Peter Pan, or Bambi?
quiz.explain: Pinocchio's wooden nose grew and grew whenever he told a fib.

quiz.prompt: Cinderella left behind a… 📖
choices: hat
coat
shoe
quiz.answer: shoe
quiz.say: When Cinderella ran home from the ball, what did she leave behind? A hat, a coat, or a shoe?
quiz.explain: She left one glass shoe on the steps, and the prince found it.

quiz.prompt: The Ugly Duckling grew into a… 📖
choices: swan
frog
bear
quiz.answer: swan
quiz.say: At the end of the story, the ugly duckling grew up into what? A swan, a frog, or a bear?
quiz.explain: He became a beautiful swan. He was never ugly at all.

lesson_media.alt: A passage detail about a character returning a lost purse branches into an inference about honesty, a question about motive, and a personal response supported by the detail.
lesson_media.caption: Talking about literature becomes stronger when a response points back to the text. One detail can support an inference, invite a question, and lead readers to compare interpretations.

nodes.title: Writing Your Own Stories
nodes.goal: Write a story with a beginning, middle and end.
nodes.kid_text: You can be the author of your very own story! Every good story has three parts: a beginning where we meet someone, a middle where a problem pops up, and an end where it gets sorted out. Start with "Once there was...", make something exciting happen, then finish it off. Grab a pencil — your imagination already has a story waiting inside it.

quiz.prompt: How many parts does a story have? 📖
quiz.say: A story has a beginning, a middle, and an end. How many parts is that? 3, 2, or 10?
quiz.explain: Three parts: a beginning, a middle, and an end.

quiz.prompt: Which words open a story? ✨
choices: Once there was
The end
And they all went home
quiz.answer: Once there was
quiz.say: Which words belong at the very beginning of a story? Once there was. The end. Or, and they all went home.
quiz.explain: Once there was opens the story and invites us to come in. The other two belong at the finish.

quiz.prompt: Where does the problem pop up?
choices: beginning
middle
end
quiz.answer: middle
quiz.say: In a story, where does the exciting problem pop up? In the beginning, the middle, or the end?
quiz.explain: The problem pops up in the middle, and it gets sorted out at the end.

quiz.prompt: Which words end a story? 📖
choices: Once
The end
Look
quiz.answer: The end
quiz.say: Which words belong on the very last line of a story? Once. The end. Or look.
quiz.explain: The end tells everybody the story is all finished.

quiz.prompt: Who makes up a story? 📖
choices: reader
chair
author
quiz.answer: author
quiz.say: The person who makes up a story and writes it down is called what? A reader, a chair, or an author?
quiz.explain: An author makes up the story, and you can be one too.

quiz.prompt: Which part comes last? 📕
choices: end
middle
start
quiz.answer: end
quiz.say: A story has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Which part comes last? The end, the middle, or the start?
quiz.explain: The end comes last, where everything gets sorted out.

quiz.prompt: First you think, then you… 💭
choices: sleep
hide
write
quiz.answer: write
quiz.say: First you think up your story. Then what do you do? Sleep, hide, or write it down?
quiz.explain: You write it down so other people can read your story too.

lesson_media.alt: A three-part story arc introduces Leo and a kite, creates the problem of the kite catching in a tree, and resolves it when a neighbor brings a ladder.
lesson_media.caption: A beginning establishes the character and situation, a middle changes that situation with a problem, and an ending shows the consequence or resolution.

nodes.title: Using a Dictionary
nodes.goal: Look up any word you meet.
nodes.kid_text: A dictionary is a giant book that knows what every word means, and it keeps them in alphabet order so you can find any one. To hunt for a word, look at its first letter and flip to that part — words starting with C live near the front, words with T live near the back. When you find it, it tells you the meaning like a helpful friend. Any word you don't know, you can now look up!

quiz.prompt: Where do C words live? 📖
choices: front
back
middle
quiz.answer: front
quiz.say: In a dictionary, words that start with C are near the front, the back, or the middle?
quiz.explain: C comes early in the alphabet, so C words live near the front.

quiz.prompt: What does a dictionary tell you?
choices: meanings
jokes
songs
quiz.answer: meanings
quiz.say: What does a dictionary tell you about a word? Its meanings, some jokes, or some songs?
quiz.explain: A dictionary tells you what a word means, like a helpful friend.

quiz.prompt: Which word comes first? 🍎🍌🍒
choices: apple
banana
cherry
quiz.answer: apple
quiz.say: In a dictionary, which word comes first? Apple, banana, or cherry?
quiz.explain: Apple starts with A, and A comes before B and C in the alphabet.

quiz.prompt: Where do Z words live? 📖
choices: back
front
middle
quiz.answer: back
quiz.say: In a dictionary, words that start with Z are near the back, the front, or the middle?
quiz.explain: Z is last in the alphabet, so Z words live right at the back.

quiz.prompt: Which word comes first? 🐶🐱🐦
choices: dog
cat
bird
quiz.answer: bird
quiz.say: In a dictionary, which word comes first? Dog, cat, or bird?
quiz.explain: Bird starts with B, and B comes before C and D in the alphabet.

quiz.prompt: What order are the words in? 📖
choices: color
ABC
size
quiz.answer: ABC
quiz.say: A dictionary keeps all its words in what order? Color order, ABC order, or size order?
quiz.explain: Words sit in ABC order, so you can always find the one you want.

quiz.prompt: Look up tiger. Hunt which letter? 🐯
choices: T
G
R
quiz.answer: T
quiz.say: You want to look up the word tiger. Which letter do you hunt for first? T, G, or R?
quiz.explain: Tiger starts with T, so you flip to the T pages.

lesson_media.alt: A lookup for cater narrows alphabetically from the C section to CA, then CAT, and finally compares cat, catch, cater and cattle in order.
lesson_media.caption: Dictionary guide words support repeated alphabetical decisions. When first letters match, compare the second, third, and later letters until the target position is determined.

nodes.title: Grammar
nodes.goal: Nouns, verbs, clauses — how sentences are engineered.

quiz.prompt: In the sentence "The clever fox quickly escaped the trap," which part of speech does the word "quickly" belong to?
quiz.answer: Adverb
quiz.explain: "Quickly" tells you how the escaping was done, so it modifies the verb — that is what an adverb does.
choices: Noun
Verb
Adverb
Adjective

quiz.prompt: Which of these sentences contains a subordinate (dependent) clause?
quiz.answer: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
quiz.explain: "Because it was raining" cannot stand alone as a sentence, so it is a subordinate clause; the other options join or contain only independent clauses or phrases.
choices: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
We stayed inside for the whole of the afternoon.
It was raining hard, and so we stayed inside.
We stayed inside and read books quietly.

quiz.prompt: In the sentence "The clever fox quickly escaped the trap," how many nouns are there?
quiz.explain: "Fox" and "trap" are the two nouns. "Clever" describes the fox (adjective), "quickly" describes the escaping (adverb), and "escaped" is the verb.

quiz.prompt: Which one of these is a complete sentence?
quiz.answer: Squirrels chattered.
choices: Squirrels chattered.
After the bell rang loudly.
Running through the wet grass.
Which the children had painted.
quiz.explain: A sentence needs a subject and a verb and must be able to stand alone. "Squirrels chattered" does; the other three are fragments — a subordinate clause, a participle phrase, and a relative clause left hanging.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence uses the verb form that matches its subject?
quiz.answer: The box of old letters was heavy.
choices: The box of old letters was heavy.
The box of old letters were heavy.
The boxes of old letters was heavy.
The box of the old letters were heavy.
quiz.explain: The subject is "box" (singular), not "letters," so the verb is "was." The words in between pull your ear towards the plural, which is exactly the trap.

quiz.prompt: You want to join "The rain stopped. We walked home." into one sentence that shows the first caused the second. Which version does that?
quiz.answer: Because the rain stopped, we walked home.
choices: The rain stopped, we walked home.
The rain stopped and we walked home.
The rain stopped; we walked home quickly.
Because the rain stopped, we walked home.
quiz.explain: "Because" is the word that states a cause. "And" and the semicolon only place the two ideas side by side, and the comma version is a comma splice — two sentences glued with a comma.

quiz.prompt: In "She handed her brother the map," what grammatical role does the word "brother" play?
quiz.answer: Indirect object
choices: Indirect object
Direct object
Subject of the verb
Object of a preposition
quiz.explain: The map is the direct object, the thing handed; the brother is the indirect object, the person it went to.

quiz.prompt: How many verbs are in this sentence: "The dog barked, ran to the gate, and waited"?
quiz.explain: Barked, ran and waited are all verbs sharing the one subject, "the dog".

quiz.prompt: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly to show that one girl owns the bicycle?
quiz.answer: The girl's bicycle was blue.
choices: The girl's bicycle was blue.
The girls bicycle was blue.
The girls' bicycle was blue.
The girls's bicycle was blue.
quiz.explain: One owner takes apostrophe + s. The form girls' would mean several girls share the bicycle.

quiz.prompt: "The old bridge over the river creaked." Name the simple subject of this sentence and explain how you found it.
quiz.answer: The simple subject is "bridge": it is the noun doing the creaking, and the words "over the river" only describe which bridge.
quiz.explain: Strip away the describing phrases and ask who or what performs the verb; the answer is the simple subject.

lesson_media.alt: A clause diagram places The fox jumps over logs at the root, then separates the noun phrase The fox from the verb phrase jumps over logs and labels their roles.
lesson_media.caption: Grammar describes relationships inside a sentence. This clause divides into a noun phrase functioning as subject and a verb phrase functioning as predicate; words form nested constituents.

nodes.title: Paragraphs and Essays
nodes.goal: Organize ideas into clear paragraphs.

quiz.prompt: A well-built paragraph usually opens with a topic sentence. What is the main job of a topic sentence?
quiz.answer: To state the main idea the other sentences support
quiz.explain: A topic sentence announces the single controlling idea, and the rest of the paragraph develops it. A hook, a definition and an essay-wide summary are all things that happen in essays — none of them is the job this sentence has.
choices: To state the main idea the other sentences support
To summarize the whole essay in one opening line
To give a surprising fact that hooks the reader
To define the words the paragraph will use

quiz.prompt: You are writing an essay and want to move from one paragraph's idea to the next. Which sentence best signals such a transition?
quiz.answer: Another reason the plan worked was its low cost.
quiz.explain: "Another reason" links the new paragraph back to the previous point and signals that an additional supporting idea is coming.
choices: In 1620 the ship finally arrived in Plymouth.
The dog in the yard was brown and very fast.
Another reason the plan worked was its low cost.
She liked green apples much more than ripe oranges.

quiz.prompt: A paragraph opens "Dogs make useful working animals." The next three sentences describe guide dogs, sheepdogs, and search-and-rescue dogs. What job are those three sentences doing in the paragraph?
quiz.answer: They are supporting details: each one gives an example that backs up the topic sentence's main idea.
quiz.explain: A topic sentence makes a claim; the sentences after it earn that claim with examples, reasons, or evidence. Three kinds of working dog are three supporting examples.

quiz.prompt: A paragraph argues that bicycles are good for crowded cities. Which sentence does NOT belong in it?
quiz.answer: My cousin's cat is named Pedals.
choices: My cousin's cat is named Pedals.
Cities with bike lanes report fewer traffic jams.
Riding a bicycle does not produce exhaust fumes.
Bicycles take up far less parking space than cars.
quiz.explain: Every sentence in a paragraph must serve the topic sentence. The cat's name is a joke about bicycles, not evidence about cities, so it breaks the paragraph's unity.

quiz.prompt: You have written the body of an essay: three paragraphs, one for each reason. What belongs in the last paragraph?
quiz.answer: A conclusion that pulls the three reasons together
choices: A conclusion that pulls the three reasons together
A summary repeating the three reasons word for word
A softening line admitting you may well be wrong
A brand-new fourth reason you did not mention
quiz.explain: A conclusion shows the reader what the three reasons add up to. Repeating them verbatim adds nothing, hedging undercuts the case you just made, and a fresh reason at the end arrives with no support behind it.

quiz.prompt: These three sentences all belong to one paragraph: "Water expands as it turns to ice." "Ice can crack a rock it has seeped into." "Pipes burst on the coldest nights." Which topic sentence fits them best?
quiz.answer: Freezing water pushes outwards, and that can break things.
choices: Ice is the solid form that water takes.
Weather affects many parts of everyday life.
Pipes sometimes burst during a very cold winter.
Freezing water pushes outwards, and that can break things.
quiz.explain: A topic sentence has to cover every detail in the paragraph and no more. "Pipes burst" covers only one detail, "weather affects life" is far too wide, and the definition of ice leaves out the breaking.

quiz.prompt: You are describing how to plant a seed, step by step. Which order should the sentences of that paragraph follow?
quiz.answer: Time order, first step to last
choices: Time order, first step to last
Shortest sentence placed first of all
The most surprising fact right at the start
Alphabetical by the tool each step uses
quiz.explain: Instructions are organized chronologically so a reader can follow along while doing the task.

quiz.prompt: In an essay, when should a writer begin a new paragraph?
quiz.answer: When the writing turns to a new idea
choices: When the writing turns to a new idea
After five sentences
Whenever a new person is mentioned by name
At the point where each written page ends
quiz.explain: A paragraph is a package for one idea, so the break comes where the idea changes, not at a fixed length.

quiz.prompt: A paragraph on why libraries matter drifts into a story about a librarian's holiday and stays there. Which fault is that?
quiz.answer: It loses unity: part of it wanders off the main idea
choices: It loses unity: part of it wanders off the main idea
It lacks a topic sentence
Its sentences are too short
It has far too many commas crowded into its long clauses
quiz.explain: Unity means everything in the paragraph serves the topic sentence; a wandering passage breaks it.

quiz.prompt: You have written a five-paragraph essay on why school lunches should change. Describe the job of your opening paragraph.
quiz.answer: The opening tells the reader what the essay will argue and gives a reason to keep reading, so it introduces the subject and states the main claim before the body paragraphs give the reasons.
quiz.explain: An introduction sets up the claim and the road ahead; the evidence belongs in the body paragraphs.

lesson_media.alt: A paragraph plan connects a topic sentence about street trees to temperature evidence, explains the shade mechanism, and links the result back to the claim.
lesson_media.caption: A coherent paragraph does more than list facts: its evidence must support the topic sentence, and its explanation must make that relevance explicit.

nodes.title: Poetry
nodes.goal: Meter, imagery, and poems worth memorizing.

quiz.prompt: Read the line: "The wind was a torrent of darkness among the gusty trees." This describes the wind as if it were a rushing flood. What poetic device is this?
quiz.answer: Metaphor
quiz.explain: Calling the wind "a torrent of darkness" states that one thing IS another without using "like" or "as," which is a metaphor.
choices: Onomatopoeia
Rhyme
Alliteration
Metaphor

quiz.prompt: A line of poetry written in iambic meter repeats a pattern of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one (da-DUM). Which phrase naturally follows this iambic rhythm?
quiz.answer: The trees are green
quiz.explain: "The TREES are GREEN" alternates unstressed-stressed twice (da-DUM da-DUM), matching the iambic pattern.
choices: Run to the store now
Elephant walking
The trees are green
Softly the snow

quiz.prompt: How many syllables are in this line of verse: "The moon is up, the stars are bright"?
quiz.explain: The / moon / is / up / the / stars / are / bright — eight syllables, four pairs of da-DUM. That is the standard length of a line of iambic tetrameter.

quiz.prompt: Read this line: "Her laughter was like a bell rolling down the hill." Which device is the poet using?
quiz.answer: Simile
choices: Simile
Metaphor
Alliteration
Personification
quiz.explain: The word "like" compares two unlike things without saying one IS the other — that is a simile. A metaphor would drop the "like" and say the laughter was a bell.

quiz.prompt: In a four-line stanza, line 1 rhymes with line 2, and line 3 rhymes with line 4. Which letters describe that rhyme scheme?
quiz.answer: AABB
choices: ABAB
ABBA
ABCB
AABB
quiz.explain: Each new rhyme sound gets the next letter, and lines that share a sound share a letter. Two rhyming pairs in a row give AABB — the scheme of most nursery rhymes.

quiz.prompt: A poem describes a street at dawn: "The morning air carried burnt toast and the sea." Which sense does this image mainly work on?
quiz.answer: Smell
choices: Sight
Touch
Taste
Smell
quiz.explain: Air "carries" toast and salt water to the nose, not the tongue or the eye. Poets build images out of all five senses, and this one is built out of smell.

quiz.prompt: Read: "The soft south wind sighed by the shore." Which sound device repeats here?
quiz.answer: Alliteration, a repeat of opening consonants
choices: Alliteration, a repeat of opening consonants
Rhyme at the line ends
A refrain that returns at the end of each stanza
A pause placed in the middle of the line of verse
quiz.explain: Five words begin with the s sound, which is alliteration.

quiz.prompt: A poem is made of six stanzas with four lines each. How many lines does the whole poem have?
quiz.explain: Six groups of four lines makes twenty-four lines in total.

quiz.prompt: A poem says "the tired old kettle grumbled on the stove." Which device gives the kettle a human quality?
quiz.answer: Personification
choices: Personification
Deliberate exaggeration
Words that imitate sounds
A repeated line or phrase
quiz.explain: Personification hands human feelings or actions to a thing; kettles do not really grumble.

quiz.prompt: Why do many poets memorise poems aloud rather than only reading them silently? Give two reasons connected to how poems are built.
quiz.answer: Poems are built out of rhythm and sound, so saying them aloud lets you hear the beat and the rhymes working, and memorising keeps the lines available to think with later.
quiz.explain: Verse is an ear-made form: much of its meaning lives in rhythm and sound that silent reading skates past.

lesson_media.alt: Three aligned panels distinguish two repeated metrical feet, a shared final sound, and the image a silver path across the sea, then connect them to an effect.
lesson_media.caption: Meter organizes stressed and unstressed syllables, sound patterning links words acoustically, and imagery evokes sensory experience. These devices can reinforce one another without being identical.

nodes.title: Myths and Legends
nodes.goal: Greek, Norse and world myths — the stories under the stories.

quiz.prompt: In Greek mythology, a mortal hero is warned by his father not to fly too high, ignores the warning out of pride, and is destroyed. This pattern of overreaching is called:
quiz.answer: Hubris
quiz.explain: Hubris is the excessive pride or defiance of the gods that repeatedly brings ruin on Greek mythological figures such as Icarus.
choices: Nemesis
Hubris
Xenia
Catharsis

quiz.prompt: Odin, Thor, and Loki belong to which mythological tradition?
quiz.answer: Norse mythology
quiz.explain: Odin, Thor, and Loki are gods of the Norse (Scandinavian) pantheon centered on Asgard.
choices: Norse mythology
Greek mythology
Roman mythology
Egyptian mythology

quiz.prompt: In the Greek myth, the craftsman Daedalus warns his son to fly a middle course, neither too low nor too high. His son ignores him. Say what happens next and what the myth is warning its listeners about.
quiz.answer: Icarus flies too near the sun, the wax holding his wings melts, and he falls into the sea; the myth warns against pride and against ignoring good advice.
quiz.explain: Greek myth punishes hubris — overreaching pride — again and again, and the punishment usually grows straight out of the fault itself. Icarus is destroyed by the very flight he was given.

quiz.prompt: Roman writers gave their own names to gods they had taken over from Greece. Which pair names the same god twice?
quiz.answer: Zeus and Jupiter
choices: Hera and Diana
Hades and Apollo
Ares and Neptune
Zeus and Jupiter
quiz.explain: Zeus and Jupiter are the same sky-father under a Greek and a Roman name. The other pairs mix up real gods: Ares matches Mars, Poseidon matches Neptune, Hera matches Juno, and Artemis matches Diana.

quiz.prompt: Cultures all over the world tell stories explaining how something in nature came to be — why the raven is black, why winter comes. Stories of that kind are called:
quiz.answer: Origin myths
choices: Fables
Riddles
Proverbs
Origin myths
quiz.explain: An origin myth explains how a feature of the world began. A fable is a short animal tale with a moral, a proverb is a saying, and a riddle is a puzzle — none of them set out to explain nature.

quiz.prompt: A story about a great flood that drowns the world, with a few survivors saved in a boat, turns up in Mesopotamian, Greek, and Hebrew tradition. What does that pattern most likely show?
quiz.answer: Stories can travel and be retold in new places
choices: Stories can travel and be retold in new places
All three peoples witnessed the same great flood
The oldest of the three versions is the true one
The three peoples must once have shared one city
quiz.explain: Neighbouring peoples traded goods and stories along the same routes, and a good story gets retold and reshaped. A shared story needs no shared city and no shared event, and an older telling is not automatically the true one.

quiz.prompt: In Norse myth, what is Ragnarok?
quiz.answer: A last battle destroying and remaking the world
choices: A last battle destroying and remaking the world
The hall of slain warriors
A war hammer the dwarves forged for the thunder god
The rainbow bridge stretching up to the world of the gods
quiz.explain: Ragnarok is the doom of the gods; Valhalla is the hall, Mjolnir the hammer, Bifrost the bridge.

quiz.prompt: The Egyptian goddess Isis, the Greek Athena and the Norse Freyja were each worshipped with temples, festivals and offerings. What does that tell us about these stories in their own time?
quiz.answer: They were living religions, not just entertaining tales
choices: They were living religions, not just entertaining tales
They were written for children to learn morals
They were invented by poets as pure fiction
They were copied from one single earlier culture's stories
quiz.explain: Myths belonged to real worship: people prayed to these gods, so the stories carried the weight of belief.

quiz.prompt: A traveller in a myth must pass a monster that kills anyone who fails to answer its question. He answers correctly and survives. Stories often use such tests to show that a hero has:
quiz.answer: wits as well as courage
choices: wits as well as courage
the favour of a particular god
royal blood in his own family
a magic sword nobody can beat
quiz.explain: Riddle tests, like the Sphinx's, prove the hero's wits: myths prize thinking as much as fighting.

quiz.prompt: The Greeks told of Prometheus stealing fire from the gods and giving it to people, and being punished terribly for it. What does this story try to explain, and what does it suggest about the gods?
quiz.answer: It explains where human fire and craft came from, and it suggests the gods guarded their powers jealously and punished anyone who shared them with people.
quiz.explain: Prometheus is an origin myth for human technology, and a warning story about defying divine power.

lesson_media.alt: Three traditions are compared without merging them: Gilgamesh confronts mortality, the Odyssey centers homecoming, and Sundiata connects a founder to communal history.
lesson_media.caption: Comparative reading can trace recurring questions while preserving cultural differences. These works arise from distinct languages, genres, performance histories, and communities.

nodes.title: Reading Novels
nodes.goal: Follow long stories; meet character, plot and setting.

quiz.prompt: In a novel, the sequence of connected events — what happens, and in what order — is called the:
quiz.answer: Plot
quiz.explain: Plot is the arrangement of events in the story; setting is where/when it happens, theme is its underlying idea, and the narrator is who tells it.
choices: Plot
Theme
Setting
Narrator

quiz.prompt: A story is told using "I woke up and knew something was wrong." From whose point of view is this narrated?
quiz.answer: First person
quiz.explain: The pronoun "I" shows a character inside the story telling it directly, which is first-person point of view.
choices: Third-person limited
Second person
First person
Third-person omniscient

quiz.prompt: A novel is narrated by a twelve-year-old boy who says "I have never told anyone this before." The book was written by a woman in her sixties. Explain who is speaking in that line and how that differs from who wrote the book.
quiz.answer: The boy is the narrator, a character invented to tell the story from inside it; the author is the real woman who wrote the book, and her voice is not the same as his.
quiz.explain: Confusing the narrator with the author is the commonest beginner's mistake in reading fiction. The narrator is part of the made-up world; the author built that world from outside it.

quiz.prompt: In a novel a girl fights to stay alive through a blizzard on a mountain, alone. The main conflict is best labelled:
quiz.answer: Character against nature
choices: Character against nature
Character against herself
Character against society
Character against another character
quiz.explain: The force working against her is the storm, so the conflict is character against nature. The other three are real kinds of conflict, but no rival, no crowd, and no inner struggle is driving this one.

quiz.prompt: Early in a novel the author mentions a loose plank on the footbridge. Forty pages later the bridge gives way under a character. That early mention is an example of:
quiz.answer: Foreshadowing
choices: Suspense
Flashback
A subplot
Foreshadowing
quiz.explain: Foreshadowing plants a detail early that pays off later. Suspense is the feeling of waiting the trick produces, a flashback jumps backwards in time, and a subplot is a second storyline.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is told from a third-person limited point of view?
quiz.answer: Mara hoped the letter had come.
choices: Mara hoped the letter had come.
I hoped the letter had come at last.
You hope the letter has come already.
Mara hoped it had come; the postman hoped so too.
quiz.explain: Third-person limited uses "he" or "she" and stays inside one character's head. "I" is first person, "you" is second person, and reaching into two characters' thoughts at once is omniscient.

quiz.prompt: Near the end of a novel the hero finally confronts the man who has been hunting her, and the outcome is decided. That moment of highest tension is the story's:
quiz.answer: climax
choices: climax
setting
resolution
exposition
quiz.explain: The climax is the turning point of greatest tension; the resolution is what settles afterwards.

quiz.prompt: A novel opens in a mining town during a long drought in 1931. All of that information is the book's:
quiz.answer: setting
choices: setting
theme
narrator
dialogue
quiz.explain: Setting is the where and when of a story, and it often shapes what can happen in it.

quiz.prompt: Early in a book a boy refuses to share anything; by the last chapter he gives away his most prized possession. Readers call a character who changes like this:
quiz.answer: a dynamic character
choices: a dynamic character
a flat, unchanging character
a minor background character
an unreliable narrator figure
quiz.explain: Dynamic characters change through the story; static characters end essentially as they began.

quiz.prompt: You are 200 pages into a long novel and have lost track of who several characters are. Describe two habits that would help you follow a long book.
quiz.answer: Keep a short list of characters with a note about each one as they appear, and read in regular chunks rather than long gaps so the plot stays fresh in your memory.
quiz.explain: Long novels reward light record-keeping and steady reading; both fight the forgetting that gaps cause.

lesson_media.alt: A novel tracker links a character's changing goal, three causally connected plot events, and a setting shift from village to city across chapters.
lesson_media.caption: Long-form reading becomes manageable when character, plot, and setting are tracked together. An event matters because it changes a goal, relationship, or later possibility.

nodes.title: Finding Things Out
nodes.goal: Use encyclopedias and libraries; check your sources.

quiz.prompt: You read a claim on a website with no author, no date, and no sources listed. What is the best next step before trusting it?
quiz.answer: Check whether independent, reliable sources agree
quiz.explain: Cross-checking a claim against independent, reliable sources is the core habit of verifying information.
choices: Reject every claim you find anywhere on the internet
Believe it because it appeared first in your search
Share it immediately so that others can decide
Check whether independent, reliable sources agree

quiz.prompt: Which source would a librarian most likely call a reliable starting point for a school report on volcanoes?
quiz.answer: An encyclopedia article with cited references
quiz.explain: What makes a starting point reliable is that it names its evidence and is edited for accuracy. A video can be excellent and still leave you nothing to check; an uncited wiki page may be right but cannot show it; and a tour company is selling something.
choices: An encyclopedia article with cited references
A popular science video with no sources listed
A wiki page whose claims carry no citations
A travel company's page about volcano tours

quiz.prompt: Two websites give different heights for the same mountain. Name two checks you could make to decide which one to trust.
quiz.answer: Check who the author is and whether the page names its evidence, and compare both figures against an official survey or an encyclopedia.
quiz.explain: Two habits settle most disputes like this: find out who is speaking and what they are relying on, then see whether an independent, reliable source gives the same figure.

quiz.prompt: For a report on the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, which of these counts as a primary source?
quiz.answer: A letter written by a survivor in 1906
choices: A letter written by a survivor in 1906
A history textbook chapter about the quake
A magazine article written a century later
An encyclopedia entry summarising the event
quiz.explain: A primary source comes from the time and place itself. The textbook, the encyclopedia, and the later article are all secondary — useful, but written by people working from other people's records.

quiz.prompt: Why does a report list its sources at the end?
quiz.answer: So a reader can check where every fact came from
choices: So a reader can check where every fact came from
So the teacher can see how many books you read
So nobody can accuse you of copying their words
So the report follows the format you were given
quiz.explain: A source list is a trail: it lets any reader go back and see whether your facts really say what you claim. Protecting yourself and satisfying the format are side effects, not the reason the convention exists.

quiz.prompt: Two search results look useful. One is a museum's own page about a fossil; the other is a blog that has copied the museum's words without saying so. Which should you cite, and why?
quiz.answer: The museum page, since that is where the facts began
choices: Whichever one you happened to open first
The museum page, since that is where the facts began
The blog post, since it is shorter and easier to read
The blog post, since it appeared higher in the results
quiz.explain: Always cite the source the information actually came from. A copy can introduce mistakes, and search ranking measures popularity, not accuracy.

quiz.prompt: In a library, non-fiction books are arranged by a number on the spine. Why is that number useful to you?
quiz.answer: It groups books by subject on the shelf
choices: It groups books by subject on the shelf
It shows how many copies the library owns
It records the order the books were bought
It tells you the reading age of the book
quiz.explain: Classification numbers group subjects, so finding one book on volcanoes lands you beside the others.

quiz.prompt: You copy three sentences from a book into your report and put your own name at the top. What should you have done instead?
quiz.answer: Quote the sentences and name the book
choices: Quote the sentences and name the book
Change two words
Write the sentences from memory instead of copying
Keep the book on a private list of your own
quiz.explain: Using someone's exact words without marking and crediting them is plagiarism; quotation plus a citation fixes it.

quiz.prompt: A page selling a brand of vitamin says the vitamin cures colds. Why should a careful researcher be cautious here?
quiz.answer: The author gains money if you believe the claim
choices: The author gains money if you believe the claim
The page was published several years ago
The writing uses long scientific words
The page shows photographs instead of graphs of data
quiz.explain: When a source profits from the claim it makes, it has a conflict of interest and needs independent checking.

quiz.prompt: You must write a report on penguins by Friday. Describe the first three steps you would take before writing a single sentence.
quiz.answer: Work out the exact question you are answering, find two or three reliable sources such as an encyclopedia and a library book, and take notes in your own words while recording where each fact came from.
quiz.explain: Research runs question first, then sources, then notes with their origins recorded so citation is easy later.

lesson_media.alt: A bridge-date question compares an archive plan, a newspaper report, and a dated museum photograph before separating construction from opening dates.
lesson_media.caption: Reliable research compares relevant, traceable sources and checks whether they are independent. Agreement is stronger when sources do not merely copy one another.

nodes.title: Where Words Come From
nodes.goal: Trace words back through history.

quiz.prompt: The English word "kindergarten" was borrowed directly from German, where it means "children's garden." A word taken from another language like this is called a:
quiz.answer: Loanword
quiz.explain: A loanword is a word adopted from another language with little or no change, such as "kindergarten" from German.
choices: Prefix
Homophone
Synonym
Loanword

quiz.prompt: The words "telephone," "telescope," and "television" all share the Greek root "tele-." Based on their meanings, "tele-" most likely means:
quiz.answer: At a distance
quiz.explain: A telephone carries voice far, a telescope sees far, and television shows distant scenes, so "tele-" means far or distant.
choices: Seeing or sight
At a distance
Small in size
Sound or voice

quiz.prompt: The English word "muscle" comes from the Latin "musculus", which means "little mouse". Suggest why Roman speakers might have chosen that word for a muscle.
quiz.answer: A muscle bunching under the skin looks like a small mouse running along beneath it, so the shape and the movement suggested the name.
quiz.explain: Many words begin as pictures. Latin speakers named the bulge in the arm after the animal it resembled, and English inherited the picture without noticing it.

quiz.prompt: English "father", German "Vater", Latin "pater", and Sanskrit "pitar" all resemble one another. The best explanation is that these languages:
quiz.answer: Grew from one older parent language
choices: Grew from one older parent language
Borrowed the word from Latin, the language of learning
Independently hit on a natural baby-talk syllable
Chose the same sounds purely by coincidence
quiz.explain: Regular sound correspondences across many languages point to a shared ancestor — here Proto-Indo-European. Latin cannot be the source, since Sanskrit was never in contact with it, and baby-talk would explain a first syllable but not the matching t and r as well.

quiz.prompt: The prefix "bi-" means two, as in "bicycle". Which of these words really does contain it with that meaning?
quiz.answer: Biannual
choices: Bison
Bishop
Bitter
Biannual
quiz.explain: Biannual means twice a year. "Bishop", "bitter", and "bison" only begin with the same two letters — a reminder that you cannot spot a root by its spelling alone.

quiz.prompt: In Shakespeare's day "awful" meant "full of awe", something grand enough to strike you silent. Today it means very bad. This shows that:
quiz.answer: Word meanings can shift over time
choices: Word meanings can shift over time
Shakespeare spelled the word wrongly
The word was borrowed from French then
People in the past used words carelessly
quiz.explain: Meaning drifts. "Awful" slid from awe-inspiring to dreadful the same way "nice" slid from foolish to pleasant — slowly, through everyday use, with nobody deciding it.

quiz.prompt: The words "port", "portable", "transport" and "import" share a Latin root. What does that root most likely mean?
quiz.answer: to carry
choices: to carry
to build
to open
to travel by sea
quiz.explain: Latin portare means to carry; a portable thing can be carried, and imports are carried in.

quiz.prompt: The word "sandwich" comes from the title of an English earl said to have eaten meat between bread so he need not leave his card table. A word made from a person's name is called:
quiz.answer: an eponym
choices: an eponym
an acronym
a synonym
a homophone
quiz.explain: Eponyms come from names: sandwich, boycott and volt are all examples.

quiz.prompt: English has both "cow" and "beef", "pig" and "pork" — the animal word from Old English, the meat word from French. Historians link this pattern to:
quiz.answer: the Norman conquest of 1066
choices: the Norman conquest of 1066
Latin taught in English monasteries
trade with the Netherlands in wool
Viking settlers in the north of England
quiz.explain: After 1066 the French-speaking nobility ate the meat while English-speaking farmers raised the animal, and both sets of words survived.

quiz.prompt: The word "computer" once meant a person who did calculations by hand. Explain what happened to this word and name the kind of change it shows.
quiz.answer: The word stayed but the thing it named changed: as machines took over the calculating, the name transferred from the person to the machine, which is an example of a word's meaning shifting over time.
quiz.explain: Semantic shift moves an old word onto a new referent rather than inventing a fresh word.

lesson_media.alt: The Latin verb portare, meaning to carry, branches through historical borrowing and word formation into portable, import and export, with prefixes changing direction.
lesson_media.caption: Etymology traces attested forms and pathways, not just visual resemblance. The English family around port reflects a borrowed Latin root, while im- and ex- contribute inward and outward senses.

nodes.title: Public Speaking
nodes.goal: Explain something you love to an audience.

quiz.prompt: You are giving a short talk about your favorite hobby to your class. Which opening is most likely to grab your audience's attention?
quiz.answer: Have you ever watched hours of work collapse in a second?
quiz.explain: Opening with a vivid question invites the audience in and sparks curiosity, unlike a flat announcement of the topic.
choices: Today I am going to talk to all of you about my favorite hobby.
Have you ever watched hours of work collapse in a second?
I was told I had to give a short speech about my hobby.
My hobby is the official topic of this classroom presentation.

quiz.prompt: During a talk, which practice best helps you connect with your audience?
quiz.answer: Making eye contact and speaking at a steady, clear pace
quiz.explain: Eye contact moved around the room, at a pace listeners can follow, is what keeps an audience with you. Reading from notes and staring at a single person are both real habits, and both leave most of the room out.
choices: Making eye contact and speaking at a steady, clear pace
Reading every word aloud from your notes without looking up
Fixing your eyes on one friendly face for the whole talk
Speaking quickly so nobody is kept waiting

quiz.prompt: A classmate ends every second sentence of her talk with "um" and keeps her eyes on her shoes. Give two pieces of advice that would most improve her next talk.
quiz.answer: Look up and make eye contact around the audience, and let a short silence stand where each "um" would go.
quiz.explain: Filler words are usually the sound of a speaker thinking, and a pause does that job better. Looking up turns a recitation into a conversation with real people.

quiz.prompt: You will show a diagram at one point in your talk. What is the best way to use it?
quiz.answer: Show it while you explain the step it illustrates
choices: Read out each label printed on it in order
Pass it round the room while you keep speaking
Hold it up at the very start and then put it away again
Show it while you explain the step it illustrates
quiz.explain: A visual aid helps when the audience sees it at the moment they need it. Passing it round splits their attention, and showing it too early or reading it aloud wastes it.

quiz.prompt: Halfway through your talk you notice that most of the class looks lost. What is the best response?
quiz.answer: Stop and explain the last point another way
choices: Stop and explain the last point another way
Ask the class to hold questions until the end
Speed up so the confusing part is over sooner
Carry on exactly as planned and hope it clears
quiz.explain: A talk is for the audience, so watching them is part of giving it. Rewording the point that lost them costs thirty seconds; pressing on loses the rest of the talk.

quiz.prompt: Which habit in the week before a talk is most likely to make it go well?
quiz.answer: Rehearsing it aloud, standing up, more than once
choices: Making the slides as detailed as you can
Rehearsing it aloud, standing up, more than once
Reading through your notes silently the night before
Writing the talk out in full and learning it by heart
quiz.explain: Speaking aloud is a different skill from reading, and only rehearsing aloud practises it. Memorised scripts collapse when one line goes missing; dense slides make the audience read instead of listen.

quiz.prompt: You have five minutes to explain how a bicycle gear works. How much material should you prepare?
quiz.answer: One idea with a few examples
choices: One idea with a few examples
Every fact you found while researching
A page of writing read out at speed
A list of ten separate short topics
quiz.explain: Short talks fail by cramming; one idea properly illustrated is what an audience can actually carry away.

quiz.prompt: A speaker rushes through her talk and finishes in half the planned time. What is the best fix for next time?
quiz.answer: Practise with a timer and pause between points
choices: Practise with a timer and pause between points
Add more slides
Speak in a much louder voice throughout the talk
Write the whole talk out word for word and read it aloud
quiz.explain: Nerves speed speech up; timed rehearsal with planned pauses trains a steadier pace.

quiz.prompt: At the end of your talk, a listener asks a question you do not know the answer to. What is the best response?
quiz.answer: Say you do not know and offer to find out
choices: Say you do not know and offer to find out
Guess an answer that sounds confident
Explain that the question is off the topic
Repeat a point you already made earlier
quiz.explain: Admitting the gap protects your credibility; inventing an answer risks losing it entirely.

quiz.prompt: You are explaining your hobby of beekeeping to people who know nothing about it. Give two things you should do so your talk makes sense to them.
quiz.answer: Explain any special words such as hive or swarm the first time you use them, and start from what the audience already knows before building up to the details.
quiz.explain: Talks fail when the speaker forgets what the audience does not yet know; define jargon and start from common ground.

lesson_media.alt: A short talk moves from a clear claim through one concrete example and an explanation to a concise takeaway directed to the audience.
lesson_media.caption: A listener can follow a talk when its signposts expose the reasoning. Evidence becomes persuasive only after the speaker explains how it supports the claim.

nodes.title: Literature
nodes.goal: Read closely: theme, symbol, voice, form.

quiz.prompt: A short story repeatedly describes a caged bird that finally sings at dawn just as an oppressed character finds her voice. The caged bird functions in the story as a:
quiz.answer: Symbol
quiz.explain: An object that carries a larger meaning beyond itself — here the bird standing for the character's constrained freedom — is a symbol.
choices: Antagonist
Rhyme scheme
Symbol
Setting

quiz.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme rather than merely a plot summary of a novel?
quiz.answer: Unchecked ambition can destroy the person who holds it.
quiz.explain: A theme is a generalizable idea about life the work explores, whereas the other options only report events that happen.
choices: A soldier returns home and marries his childhood friend.
A detective interviews six suspects over three days.
Unchecked ambition can destroy the person who holds it.
The family moves to a new city early in the spring.

quiz.prompt: A critic praises a poem for its distinctive "voice." In literary analysis, a work's voice most nearly refers to:
quiz.answer: The tone and personality projected by the speaker
quiz.explain: Voice is the attitude and personality a text projects through diction, syntax and tone. Metre, rhyme and date are all real features of a poem, and none of them is what a critic means by praising its voice.
choices: The historical period in which the poem was written
The tone and personality projected by the speaker
The number of syllables counted in every line
Whether the poem rhymes and how regular it is

quiz.prompt: A narrator describes a landlord who has just evicted a widow in midwinter, and remarks: "He was, of course, a most generous man." Everything the story shows says otherwise. Name the technique and explain how a reader detects it.
quiz.answer: It is verbal irony: the narrator's words state the opposite of what is meant, and the reader detects it because the events of the story contradict the compliment.
quiz.explain: Verbal irony needs two things the reader can compare: what is said, and what the text elsewhere shows to be true. The gap between them carries the real judgement.

quiz.prompt: A narrator describes a character's room as "a cell of a bedroom, its one window barred by the fire escape." The word choice builds a strong sense of:
quiz.answer: Confinement
choices: Nostalgia
Prosperity
Playfulness
Confinement
quiz.explain: "Cell" and "barred" belong to the vocabulary of prison, and a writer's diction colours a scene before any event happens. Close reading means noticing which word was chosen over its neighbours.

quiz.prompt: A poem runs to fourteen lines of iambic pentameter and turns sharply in argument after line eight. Its form is:
quiz.answer: A sonnet
choices: A ballad
An ode
A haiku
A sonnet
quiz.explain: Fourteen lines, five iambs each, with a volta after the octave: that is the sonnet, in its Italian shape. A ballad is a rhymed story in quatrains, and an ode is a long address with no fixed length.

quiz.prompt: A novel's narrator insists he behaved honourably, yet every scene he describes shows him lying to his friends. A reader should conclude that the book has:
quiz.answer: an unreliable narrator whose account we must read against
choices: an unreliable narrator whose account we must read against
a third-person omniscient point of view
a badly constructed plot with contradictions
an author who plainly shares the narrator's view of his own conduct
quiz.explain: When the evidence of a text undercuts its teller, the gap is a deliberate device, and it becomes the reader's job to judge.

quiz.prompt: A poem describes a battlefield with short, clipped lines and hard consonants; a later poem on the same subject uses long, flowing lines. What are the poets chiefly varying?
quiz.answer: form, which shapes how the subject feels to the reader
choices: form, which shapes how the subject feels to the reader
theme, since the subject matter is different
plot, since the events described are different
genre, since one is verse and one is prose
quiz.explain: Both have the same subject; the difference lies in formal choices of line and sound, and form carries meaning.

quiz.prompt: A story is told entirely through one character's unpunctuated rush of memories and half-thoughts as she waits for a train. This technique is:
quiz.answer: stream of consciousness
choices: stream of consciousness
a dramatic monologue in verse
an omniscient survey of minds
epistolary narration in letters
quiz.explain: Stream of consciousness reproduces the flow of a mind rather than an ordered account of events.

quiz.prompt: A reader says the theme of a novel is "a boy runs away from home and joins a circus." Explain why that is not a theme, and show how to turn it into one.
quiz.answer: That is plot, a summary of events; a theme is the idea the events explore, so it would become something like a claim that escape from one cage often leads into another.
quiz.explain: Plot answers what happens; theme answers what the happening means, stated as an idea that could be argued.

lesson_media.alt: A repeated locked-door image connects two quoted details to a pattern of exclusion and then to a qualified thematic interpretation about belonging.
lesson_media.caption: Close reading moves from observable language to pattern and interpretation. A theme is an argued meaning supported by multiple details, not a hidden label attached to one symbol.

nodes.title: Shakespeare
nodes.goal: Read a comedy and a tragedy in the original.

quiz.prompt: Shakespeare's plays are commonly sorted into three genres. A play that ends with the death of its noble protagonist, brought down partly by his own flaw, is classified as a:
quiz.answer: Tragedy
quiz.explain: A Shakespearean tragedy centers on a high-status protagonist whose fatal flaw leads to his downfall and death, as in Hamlet or Macbeth.
choices: Comedy
Tragedy
History
Sonnet

quiz.prompt: In Hamlet's line "To be, or not to be, that is the question," Hamlet is chiefly weighing:
quiz.answer: Whether to go on living or to escape into death
quiz.explain: The soliloquy meditates on existence versus death — enduring life's pains or escaping them — which is why "to be, or not to be" frames the choice of living against dying.
choices: Whether to become king or stay a mere soldier
Whether he can trust his old friend Horatio
Whether to go on living or to escape into death
Whether to marry Ophelia or flee away from Denmark
