quiz.prompt: Shakespeare often wrote his dialogue in unrhymed iambic pentameter. This form is called:
quiz.answer: Blank verse
quiz.explain: Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter; free verse has no set meter, prose has no line structure, and heroic couplets rhyme.
choices: Prose
Blank verse
Free verse
Heroic couplets

quiz.prompt: In Macbeth, the audience has just heard the Macbeths plan a murder when King Duncan arrives and praises the castle's pleasant air. Name the technique this creates and explain what it does to the scene.
quiz.answer: Dramatic irony: the audience knows what Duncan does not, so his praise of the castle becomes ominous and the scene fills with tension instead of welcome.
quiz.explain: Dramatic irony works on the gap between what the audience knows and what the character knows. Shakespeare uses it to make an ordinary courtesy unbearable to watch.

quiz.prompt: Alone on an empty stage, a character speaks his private thoughts aloud with no one to hear them. In a Shakespeare play that speech is:
quiz.answer: A soliloquy
choices: An aside
A prologue
A dialogue
A soliloquy
quiz.explain: A soliloquy is a character thinking aloud, alone. An aside is a quick remark thrown to the audience while other characters are present, and a prologue is spoken before the action begins.

quiz.prompt: Twelfth Night ends with mistaken identities untangled, three couples married, and nobody dead. By the conventions of Shakespeare's own age, the play is:
quiz.answer: A comedy
choices: A comedy
A history
A romance
A tragedy
quiz.explain: Shakespearean comedy is defined by its ending — confusion resolved and marriages made — not by how funny it is. Histories dramatise English kings, and tragedies end in the protagonist's death.

quiz.prompt: In Shakespeare's theatre, low-status or comic characters often speak in prose while nobles speak in verse. A noble character who suddenly drops into prose is most likely signalling:
quiz.answer: a collapse of composure or a change of state
choices: a collapse of composure or a change of state
that the character is quoting someone of lower rank
an error introduced by the printer of the text
the arrival of a new subplot with comic characters
quiz.explain: The verse-prose switch is a dramatic signal: madness, disguise or intimacy often pushes a noble into prose. Quotation, compositor error and a change of plot line are all real possibilities in an early text, but none of them is what the convention marks.

quiz.prompt: The Globe had no artificial lighting, no curtain and almost no scenery. What follows for how Shakespeare wrote?
quiz.answer: Characters describe place and time in the dialogue itself
choices: Characters describe place and time in the dialogue itself
Actors announced each scene's location before entering
Scenes were kept short so sets could be moved
Plays were performed after dark by torchlight
quiz.explain: Lines such as "But look, the morn in russet mantle clad" paint the scenery that the bare stage could not. There was no announcer, nothing to move, and no lighting — which is exactly why performances ran in the afternoon.

quiz.prompt: In Romeo and Juliet the Prologue tells the audience at the start that the lovers will die. Why would a playwright give away the ending?
quiz.answer: It shifts attention from what happens to how it happens
choices: It shifts attention from what happens to how it happens
It matches the source story the audience already knew
It shortens the play by removing the suspense
It signals that the play is a comedy
quiz.explain: Knowing the doom makes each hopeful moment painful; the interest moves to the machinery of the tragedy. The audience did know the story from Brooke's poem, but a familiar plot does not have to be announced — Shakespeare announces it because he wants the dread working from line one.

quiz.prompt: A student complains that Shakespeare's language is impossible and gives up on the first page. Suggest two practical approaches that make an early modern play readable.
quiz.answer: Read it aloud, or watch a performance, because the lines were written to be spoken and much of the sense comes through in the acting, and use footnotes to check the handful of words whose meanings have changed rather than stopping at every unfamiliar phrase.
quiz.explain: The plays are scripts, not novels; hearing them and glossing shifted vocabulary removes most of the difficulty.

lesson_media.alt: Two dramatic structures are contrasted: a comedy moves from blocked relationships through recognition to social reunion, while a tragedy moves from choice through reversal to irreversible loss.
lesson_media.caption: Shakespearean comedies and tragedies vary, but genre expectations shape audience inference. Comic recognition often enables renewed social order; tragic action makes loss difficult or impossible to undo.

nodes.title: World Literature
nodes.goal: Read beyond your borders: epics and classics of many cultures.

quiz.prompt: "One Thousand and One Nights" is built around Scheherazade, who tells the king a story each night, often stopping at a cliffhanger. This structure — stories nested inside a wrapping story — is called a:
quiz.answer: Frame narrative
quiz.explain: A frame narrative embeds tales within an outer story (the frame), exactly as Scheherazade's nightly stories sit inside the tale of her and the king.
choices: Dramatic monologue
Sonnet sequence
Frame narrative
Epistolary novel

quiz.prompt: Epics such as the Mesopotamian "Epic of Gilgamesh" and the Indian "Mahabharata" share which typical feature?
quiz.answer: A long narrative poem of a nation's heroic deeds
quiz.explain: Epic poetry is defined as a lengthy narrative recounting the heroic deeds central to a culture, a form found across many traditions.
choices: A collection of unrelated proverbs and sayings
A long narrative poem of a nation's heroic deeds
A private diary of daily life written in prose
A short humorous poem written to be sung out loud

quiz.prompt: Reading literature in translation from many cultures primarily helps a reader to:
quiz.answer: Compare human experience across unfamiliar traditions
quiz.explain: World literature broadens a reader by setting traditions beside one another. It does not flatten them into one story, it is not a competition, and reading in translation is a way into other languages rather than an excuse from them.
choices: Compare human experience across unfamiliar traditions
Meet the same story told in slightly different words
Decide which tradition has produced the finest work
Avoid having to learn another language at all

quiz.prompt: The Epic of Gilgamesh, the Odyssey, and the Ramayana were all shaped by performers long before anyone wrote them down. Name two features of such poems that point to oral composition, and say why each helps a performer.
quiz.answer: Repeated set phrases and stock scenes, and a strong regular rhythm: the formulas give the singer ready-made pieces that fit the line, and the rhythm carries the memory forward.
quiz.explain: A poem composed in performance must be rebuilt every time it is sung. Repeated epithets, recurring scenes and a fixed metre are the tools that make that possible.

quiz.prompt: A West African griot performs a long praise-poem about a king's ancestors from memory at a festival, as griots in his family have done for generations. Which claim about this poem is best supported?
quiz.answer: It belongs to a living oral tradition, not a lost one
choices: It belongs to a living oral tradition, not a lost one
It is fixed word for word and never varies in performance
It was probably composed by a single named author
It is folklore rather than literature of any kind
quiz.explain: Oral literature is not a stage that cultures grow out of — griot performance is a living, trained art. Its texts are rebuilt at each performance rather than fixed, and shaped over generations rather than by one author.

quiz.prompt: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart takes its title from a poem by W. B. Yeats and tells an Igbo story in English, for readers who had mostly met Africa in European novels. Critics usually read this combination as:
quiz.answer: Writing back to a colonial literary tradition
choices: Copying the plot of a Yeats poem
A translation of a Yeats poem into a novel
Abandoning Igbo culture in favour of English
Writing back to a colonial literary tradition
quiz.explain: Achebe took the coloniser's language and literary forms and turned them to tell the story from inside the Igbo world — a move critics call writing back.

quiz.prompt: A Japanese haiku translated into English loses its 5-7-5 sound pattern but keeps its image. What does this show about reading in translation?
quiz.answer: Some features survive translation and others are lost
choices: Some features survive translation and others are lost
A translated poem counts as a new work by the translator
The translator should have forced 5-7-5 into English
A haiku is defined above all by its syllable count
quiz.explain: Imagery often crosses languages; sound patterns tied to the original's phonology usually do not. Japanese counts sound units rather than English syllables, so forcing 5-7-5 into English reproduces a number, not the form.

quiz.prompt: Latin American writers such as Gabriel Garcia Marquez tell stories in which a woman ascends to heaven while hanging out sheets, and the villagers treat it as ordinary. This mode is known as:
quiz.answer: magical realism
choices: magical realism
the picaresque novel
literary naturalism
high epic fantasy
quiz.explain: Magical realism embeds impossible events in a realistic world without astonishment, unlike fantasy's separate secondary world.

quiz.prompt: Two translations of the same Russian novel differ noticeably in tone. What is the best conclusion for a reader comparing them?
quiz.answer: Each translator made interpretive choices worth examining
choices: Each translator made interpretive choices worth examining
One translator must have misunderstood the Russian
The original novel had two different versions
Whichever is more recent will be more accurate
quiz.explain: Translation is interpretation; comparing versions exposes decisions about register, rhythm and idiom.

quiz.prompt: A reader says the Odyssey feels strange because Odysseus lies constantly yet is admired. Explain how reading a work in its own cultural context helps here.
quiz.answer: The values of the poem's own society are not ours: cunning and clever deception were admired Greek virtues in a hero, so what looks like a moral flaw to a modern reader was a strength to the original audience.
quiz.explain: Judging a text only by present-day values misreads it; reconstructing its own value system is part of the work.

lesson_media.alt: An epic comparison aligns the Epic of Gilgamesh, Mahabharata and Sundiata by transmission form, central question and cultural setting rather than treating them as interchangeable.
lesson_media.caption: World literature requires both comparison and context. Translation and circulation make texts travel, but form, performance, and historical setting continue to shape what each work means.

nodes.title: Rhetoric
nodes.goal: Ethos, pathos, logos — the machinery of persuasion.

quiz.prompt: A speaker argues: "As a doctor with thirty years treating this disease, I can tell you this treatment is safe." Which mode of persuasion is she primarily using?
quiz.answer: Ethos
quiz.explain: By citing her credentials and experience to establish credibility, she appeals through ethos, the appeal from the speaker's character or authority.
choices: Logos
Ethos
Kairos
Pathos

quiz.prompt: An advertisement shows a shivering, hungry child and asks, "How can you look away?" This appeal works chiefly through:
quiz.answer: Pathos
quiz.explain: Stirring the audience's emotions — pity and guilt — to persuade is pathos, the appeal to feeling.
choices: Pathos
Logos
Ethos
Syntax

quiz.prompt: Which argument relies most directly on logos?
quiz.answer: The bridge holds 40 tons, so only four 10-ton trucks fit.
quiz.explain: Logos persuades through reasoning and evidence; the load-and-weight calculation is a logical argument rather than an appeal to character or emotion.
choices: The bridge holds 40 tons, so only four 10-ton trucks fit.
Any true patriot would surely agree with me on this.
Think of all the families who will suffer if we fail here.
Trust me, I have never once steered you wrong before.

quiz.prompt: A campaign advertisement says: "Every parent wants safe streets. My opponent voted against the police budget. Ask yourself who really cares about your children." Name the chief appeal it uses and state what the argument leaves out.
quiz.answer: The chief appeal is pathos — fear for children — and it leaves out any evidence that the vote actually made streets less safe.
quiz.explain: Emotional appeals are not fallacies in themselves; they become one when they stand in for the missing link in the argument. Here nothing connects a single budget vote to street safety.

quiz.prompt: A speaker begins: "We have waited ten years. We have written letters. We have marched. We have been patient." The repeated opening phrase is a figure called:
quiz.answer: Anaphora
choices: Anaphora
Hyperbole
Euphemism
Antithesis
quiz.explain: Anaphora repeats the same words at the start of successive clauses to build rhythm and pressure. Antithesis balances opposites, hyperbole exaggerates, and euphemism softens.

quiz.prompt: A debater answers the proposal "we should limit lorry speeds near schools" with "my opponent wants to ban all lorries from the roads." This move is:
quiz.answer: A straw man
choices: A straw man
An ad hominem
A false dilemma
A slippery slope
quiz.explain: A straw man replaces the real proposal with a weaker, invented one and then knocks that down. A slippery slope would instead claim the limit leads step by step to a ban.

quiz.prompt: A columnist writes: "Either we build this motorway or the region dies." What is wrong with the reasoning?
quiz.answer: It offers two options where more in fact exist
choices: It offers two options where more in fact exist
It relies on the authority of the writer
It attacks the character of an opponent
It appeals to the reader's emotions rather than to facts
quiz.explain: This is a false dilemma: the argument hides the middle ground of other possible policies.

quiz.prompt: A speaker asks "Are we really going to let this stand?" and moves on without waiting for an answer. This figure is:
quiz.answer: a rhetorical question
choices: a rhetorical question
an antithesis
an allusion to another text
a deliberate hyperbole
quiz.explain: A rhetorical question makes an assertion in question form, drawing the audience into supplying the answer.

quiz.prompt: Someone argues "Sales of ice cream and cases of sunburn rise together, so ice cream must cause sunburn." Diagnose the flaw.
quiz.answer: Two things rising together may share a common cause
choices: Two things rising together may share a common cause
The evidence comes from too small a sample
The speaker has misdefined the key term
The conclusion restates the premise itself
quiz.explain: Correlation is not causation: hot weather drives both figures up.

quiz.prompt: A campaign speech uses strong ethos and pathos but almost no logos. Predict how a hostile, well-informed audience will respond, and say why.
quiz.answer: They will find it unpersuasive and may feel manipulated, because an audience that already doubts the speaker's credibility will not accept ethos, and without evidence or reasoning there is nothing left for them to test or agree with.
quiz.explain: The three appeals work together; a sceptical audience demands logos because ethos alone has no purchase on them.

lesson_media.alt: One proposal to add a crossing is supported three ways: ethos cites an engineer, pathos evokes a child's risky walk, and logos compares traffic counts and stopping distance.
lesson_media.caption: Ethos concerns credibility, pathos addresses emotion, and logos develops reasoning. They can work together, but none excuses false evidence or an invalid inference.

nodes.title: The Essay
nodes.goal: Write arguments that are clear, honest and alive.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence works best as an arguable thesis for a persuasive essay?
quiz.answer: School should start later because teens need more sleep.
quiz.explain: A strong thesis states a specific, debatable claim and previews the reasoning, unlike a mere topic announcement.
choices: School should start later because teens need more sleep.
This essay is about the topic of school start times.
Many people have opinions about when school should start.
School start times are an interesting topic to consider.

quiz.prompt: You are writing an argument and address the strongest objection to your position before refuting it. This move is called:
quiz.answer: Addressing a counterargument
quiz.explain: Acknowledging and responding to an opposing view is called handling the counterargument, and it strengthens an honest argument.
choices: Citing a supporting source
Committing a straw man fallacy
Addressing a counterargument
Restating the thesis again

quiz.prompt: A writer argues: "Everyone I know supports this law, so it must be what the whole country wants." This reasoning is flawed because it:
quiz.answer: Generalizes from a small, unrepresentative sample
quiz.explain: Inferring a nationwide view from the writer's personal circle is a hasty generalization. The argument never actually claims majorities are right — it claims, wrongly, to know what the majority thinks.
choices: Generalizes from a small, unrepresentative sample
Confuses what people want with what is good for them
Relies on the writer's own authority as the evidence
Assumes that a majority view must be correct

quiz.prompt: A student's body paragraph gives three quotations one after another and then moves on. Say what is missing and why it matters to the argument.
quiz.answer: Analysis is missing: the writer has to explain how each quotation supports the claim, otherwise the evidence just sits there and the claim is never actually argued.
quiz.explain: Quotation is not argument. Evidence only counts once the writer shows what it proves, which is the sentence most weak paragraphs leave out.

quiz.prompt: An essay claims that early start times harm learning, and has the raw fact that the school day begins at 07:40. Which sentence best turns that fact into evidence?
quiz.answer: Teenagers need about nine hours' sleep, so a 07:40 start cuts into it.
choices: Most students say they dislike getting up before dawn.
Some schools in other countries start at 09:00 instead.
The school day starts at 07:40, which is very early indeed.
Teenagers need about nine hours' sleep, so a 07:40 start cuts into it.
quiz.explain: A fact becomes evidence only when it is joined to the claim by a reason. Repeating the fact, polling opinion, or naming another country leaves the join unmade.

quiz.prompt: An essay asserts that "screens destroy attention." A reader suggests qualifying the claim. Which revision qualifies it rather than simply retreating from it?
quiz.answer: Heavy screen use is linked to shorter sustained attention in several studies.
choices: Screens do not affect attention in any real way.
Many people believe screens are bad for attention.
Screens may possibly perhaps harm attention in some way.
Heavy screen use is linked to shorter sustained attention in several studies.
quiz.explain: Qualifying means narrowing a claim to what your evidence supports — who, how much, on what basis. Piling on hedges or handing the claim to "many people" abandons it instead.

quiz.prompt: A student's essay says "there are many views on this important topic" three times in different paragraphs. What should the revision do?
quiz.answer: Replace the filler with a claim and evidence
choices: Replace the filler with a claim and evidence
Move the sentences to the conclusion
Add another paragraph listing the views themselves
Shorten each sentence by cutting its adjectives
quiz.explain: Sentences that could top any essay on any topic carry no argument; specificity is what makes writing say something.

quiz.prompt: An essay's paragraphs are each sound but the reader cannot see how paragraph three follows from paragraph two. What is the essay missing?
quiz.answer: Signposting that shows how each step connects
choices: Signposting that shows how each step connects
A stronger opening sentence in each one
More quotations from published sources
A shorter and punchier concluding line
quiz.explain: Coherence is the reader's sense of a chain; explicit connective work makes the argument's structure visible.

quiz.prompt: A writer wants to concede a point without abandoning the argument. Which sentence does that?
quiz.answer: Although the costs are real, they are outweighed by the savings.
choices: Although the costs are real, they are outweighed by the savings.
Some people believe the costs are far too high.
The costs are genuinely too high to justify this.
Nobody has ever proved that the costs are high.
quiz.explain: A concession grants the opposing point in a subordinate clause and then subordinates it to the main claim.

quiz.prompt: A first draft argues its case well but reads as a list of assertions with no sources. Describe two revisions that would strengthen it and say what each adds.
quiz.answer: Attach specific evidence such as figures, examples or cited studies to each claim, which lets a reader check the reasoning rather than trust it, and add a paragraph engaging the strongest objection, which shows the argument survives testing.
quiz.explain: An argument earns belief by being checkable and by surviving the best case against it.

lesson_media.alt: A five-step essay map links a qualified thesis to source evidence, an explicit warrant, a cost counterargument, and a bounded pilot-study conclusion.
lesson_media.caption: An argument earns its conclusion by making warrants visible and confronting relevant objections. Qualification is a strength when the evidence supports a limited claim.

nodes.title: How Language Works
nodes.goal: Phonemes, morphemes, syntax — language as a natural system.

quiz.prompt: The smallest unit of sound that can distinguish one word from another — such as the difference between "pat" and "bat" — is called a:
quiz.answer: Phoneme
quiz.explain: A phoneme is the smallest contrastive sound unit; swapping /p/ for /b/ changes "pat" to "bat," showing they are distinct phonemes.
choices: Phoneme
Morpheme
Grapheme
Syntax

quiz.prompt: How many morphemes does the word "unhappiness" contain?
quiz.explain: "Unhappiness" breaks into un- + happy + -ness, three meaningful units, so it has three morphemes.

quiz.prompt: The rules that govern how words combine into grammatical sentences in a language are the domain of:
quiz.answer: Syntax
quiz.explain: Syntax studies how words are arranged into phrases and sentences; phonology handles sound, morphology word-structure, and semantics meaning.
choices: Syntax
Phonology
Semantics
Morphology

quiz.prompt: The word "thought" is written with seven letters. How many distinct speech sounds (phonemes) does it actually contain?
quiz.explain: "Thought" is /θ/ + /ɔː/ + /t/: the "th" spells one sound, "ough" spells one vowel, and the final "t" is the third. English spelling and English sound are two different systems.

quiz.prompt: Which of these pairs of English words is a minimal pair?
quiz.answer: ship / sheep
choices: ship / boat
ship / sheep
sheep / sheeps
shop / shopping
quiz.explain: A minimal pair differs in exactly one sound in the same position — here the vowel, /ɪ/ against /iː/. "Ship/boat" differ in meaning but in every sound, and the other two pairs differ by whole added morphemes.

quiz.prompt: English speakers add [s] to "cat", [z] to "dog", and [ɪz] to "horse" without ever being taught to. This shows that the plural rule is:
quiz.answer: Applied automatically according to the preceding sound
choices: A spelling rule with no effect on pronunciation
Borrowed from Latin along with the plural ending
Learned separately for each individual English word
Applied automatically according to the preceding sound
quiz.explain: The ending changes to match the sound before it, and speakers do it to invented words too — say "three wugs" aloud and you will produce [z]. That is a rule, not a list.

quiz.prompt: A four-year-old says "I holded the rabbit" though nobody has ever said that to her. What does this error reveal?
quiz.answer: She has internalised a rule and is extending it
choices: She has internalised a rule and is extending it
She is copying an adult's mistake
She has not yet learned the past tense forms of verbs
She is confusing two different verbs with each other
quiz.explain: Overregularisation is evidence of rule learning: the child applies the regular -ed rule to an irregular verb she cannot have heard.

quiz.prompt: In one language the verb comes at the end of the sentence; in another it sits between subject and object. Linguists describe this as a difference in:
quiz.answer: word order
choices: word order
morphology
phonology
semantics
quiz.explain: Word order is a syntactic parameter; Japanese is verb-final where English is subject-verb-object.

quiz.prompt: A dictionary editor argues that "literally" now also means "figuratively" because speakers use it that way. She is taking which stance?
quiz.answer: a descriptive one, recording how the language is used
choices: a descriptive one, recording how the language is used
a prescriptive one, defending the older rule
an etymological one, tracing the word's origin
a phonetic one, describing how it is said
quiz.explain: Descriptive linguistics reports usage; prescriptivism rules on what usage ought to be.

quiz.prompt: How many distinct speech sounds (phonemes) does the word "straight" contain?
quiz.explain: The eight letters spell just five sounds: s, t, r, the vowel, and t.

lesson_media.alt: The utterance Cats sleep is analyzed from contrasting speech sounds to the plural morpheme cat plus s, then the noun phrase and verb phrase, and finally its compositional meaning.
lesson_media.caption: Language is organized at interacting levels. Phonemes distinguish forms, morphemes contribute meaning or grammar, syntax combines constituents, and semantics interprets the result.

nodes.title: Media Literacy
nodes.goal: Read the news like a critic: bias, framing, evidence.

quiz.prompt: Two newspapers report the same protest. One headline reads "Citizens demand justice"; the other reads "Mob disrupts city center." The difference between these headlines best illustrates:
quiz.answer: Framing
quiz.explain: Selecting words that shape how the same event is perceived — heroic citizens versus a disruptive mob — is framing.
choices: Typography
Framing
Circulation
Fact-checking

quiz.prompt: A news article states a striking statistic but names no study, agency, or source. A media-literate reader should:
quiz.answer: Treat it cautiously and look for the original source
quiz.explain: Unsourced claims should be verified against their original evidence before being trusted.
choices: Accept it because it is printed in a real newspaper
Share it widely because the number is memorable
Treat it cautiously and look for the original source
Assume it is false and ignore the rest of the article

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is the clearest sign that a piece is opinion/editorial rather than straight news reporting?
quiz.answer: It urges readers to support a policy in persuasive language
quiz.explain: Advocating a position with persuasive language marks opinion writing, whereas straight news attributes verifiable facts to sources.
choices: It reports the time, place, and confirmed toll of an event
It presents figures drawn from an official government report
It quotes multiple named officials and attributes each fact
It urges readers to support a policy in persuasive language

quiz.prompt: A headline reads "400% RISE IN SHARK ATTACKS". Paragraph nine says the number went from one attack to five. Explain what is misleading and how you would report the same finding honestly.
quiz.answer: The percentage hides how small the numbers are; an honest report gives the actual figures — five attacks this year against one last year — so readers can judge the size for themselves.
quiz.explain: Percentages of tiny base numbers produce enormous-sounding changes. The fix is not to ban percentages but to print the raw counts beside them.

quiz.prompt: A striking statistic is circulating online. Which question best tests whether it can be trusted?
quiz.answer: Who collected the figure, and how?
choices: Who collected the figure, and how?
Does the website look professionally designed?
How many people have shared the post so far?
Does the figure match what I already believe?
quiz.explain: Trust follows the method and the source, not the design or the share count. Checking a number against your own expectations is how confirmation bias gets in.

quiz.prompt: A news report writes "the minister admitted that costs had risen" where it could have written "said". What does the choice of "admitted" do?
quiz.answer: It implies guilt or reluctance that "said" does not
choices: It marks the sentence as a direct quotation
It shows the minister spoke louder than usual
It reports the same neutral fact more precisely
It implies guilt or reluctance that "said" does not
quiz.explain: Reporting verbs carry judgements: admitted, conceded, claimed and insisted all colour the same statement differently. Neutral reporting sticks to "said".

quiz.prompt: A news website publishes a story an hour after a crash, then quietly changes three facts the next morning without a note. What should a careful reader conclude?
quiz.answer: Early reports are provisional and should be rechecked
choices: Early reports are provisional and should be rechecked
The outlet is deliberately spreading falsehoods
The original journalist invented the details
Online news is inherently less accurate than printed news
quiz.explain: Breaking coverage is written under uncertainty; the honest practice is to log corrections, and the reader's is to revisit.

quiz.prompt: A newspaper runs a full front page on knife crime for a week. Crime figures have not changed. What effect does this coverage most likely have?
quiz.answer: It raises how important readers judge the issue to be
choices: It raises how important readers judge the issue to be
It changes what readers believe about the facts
It reduces the paper's sales among its readers
It causes an actual increase in the crime rate
quiz.explain: This is agenda setting: repeated coverage shapes what audiences think about, distinct from what they think.

quiz.prompt: A reader only follows accounts that share her politics and finds every post confirms her view. The likeliest explanation is:
quiz.answer: her feed has been narrowed to agreeable sources
choices: her feed has been narrowed to agreeable sources
the opposing evidence has been suppressed
her view is supported by the whole public
the platform has stopped ranking content
quiz.explain: Self-selection plus algorithmic ranking produces a filter bubble in which agreement looks like consensus.

quiz.prompt: A photograph of a half-empty square is captioned "protest fizzles." Explain two questions a media-literate reader should ask before accepting that story.
quiz.answer: When and from what angle was the photograph taken, since a shot early in the day or from one corner can show an empty square at a full protest, and what independent estimates of the crowd exist from police, organisers or other outlets.
quiz.explain: A photograph is a selection of one moment and one viewpoint; corroboration from other sources tests the caption's claim.

lesson_media.alt: The same outcome of 90 successes among 100 trials is framed as a 90 percent success headline and a 10 percent failure headline, both pointing back to one data table.
lesson_media.caption: Framing changes emphasis without necessarily changing the underlying numbers. A critical reader returns to the denominator, method, source, and omitted comparison before judging either headline.

nodes.title: A Second Language
nodes.goal: Begin another language and keep it alive daily.

quiz.prompt: A learner of Spanish says "Yo tengo hambre" perfectly but freezes when asked to invent a new sentence on the spot. This gap illustrates the difference between:
quiz.answer: Memorized formulas versus productive grammar
quiz.explain: Producing a rehearsed phrase does not require the generative grammatical ability needed to build novel sentences, a well-known distinction in second-language acquisition.
choices: Reading comprehension versus listening skill
Vocabulary size versus accurate pronunciation
Formal register versus informal register
Memorized formulas versus productive grammar

quiz.prompt: Research on second-language acquisition suggests that which practice most supports keeping a new language alive?
quiz.answer: Frequent, regular exposure and use spread over time
quiz.explain: Consistent, distributed practice and meaningful use are far more effective for retention than a single cram session.
choices: Avoiding mistakes by speaking as little as possible
Cramming all the grammar rules once before a single exam
Frequent, regular exposure and use spread over time
Translating word-for-word from the first language

quiz.prompt: A French speaker learning English keeps saying "I have 20 years" for their age, mirroring French "j'ai 20 ans." This error most likely comes from:
quiz.answer: First-language transfer
quiz.explain: The speaker is carrying the structure of their first language into the new one — first-language transfer, a core idea in second-language acquisition. English marks age with "be", French with "have".
choices: Limited French vocabulary
A mild hearing problem
First-language transfer
Random guessing at words

quiz.prompt: You have memorised 500 French words but freeze whenever a real conversation starts. Describe two changes to your practice that research on language learning supports, and say why each helps.
quiz.answer: Practise regularly in short sessions rather than in one long block, and spend the time listening and speaking in real conversation, because the language is retained by spaced use and built by producing it under pressure.
quiz.explain: Vocabulary lists build recognition; conversation builds retrieval. Spacing practice across days beats massing it, and speaking is the only practice that rehearses speaking.

quiz.prompt: A Spanish speaker learning English says "I am embarrassed" meaning "I am pregnant", because Spanish "embarazada" means pregnant. Pairs of words like this are called:
quiz.answer: False friends
choices: Cognates
Loanwords
Homophones
False friends
quiz.explain: False friends look like translations of each other and are not. They are often genuine cognates that drifted apart in meaning, which is exactly why they catch learners out.

quiz.prompt: A learner watches Spanish television with Spanish subtitles for an hour a day, understanding a little more each month, and rarely looks anything up. This practice is closest to what researchers call:
quiz.answer: Comprehensible input
choices: Error correction
Rote memorisation
Grammar translation
Comprehensible input
quiz.explain: Comprehensible input is language just beyond your current level that context makes understandable. It is the opposite of grammar-translation drilling, and it does most of its work without explicit correction.

quiz.prompt: A learner reviews vocabulary the day after learning it, then three days later, then a week later. This schedule is designed to exploit:
quiz.answer: spaced repetition, which strengthens recall over time
choices: spaced repetition, which strengthens recall over time
immersion in the target language environment
the critical period for language learning
interference carried over from the learner's first language
quiz.explain: Reviewing just as an item starts to fade produces stronger retention than massed study of the same total length.

quiz.prompt: Two learners study German for a year. One drills grammar alone; the other talks weekly with a German friend. Predict the likeliest difference in their speaking.
quiz.answer: The second speaks more fluently under real-time pressure
choices: The second speaks more fluently under real-time pressure
The first speaks with fewer errors and more ease
Both will speak at almost exactly the same level
The second will know far fewer grammar rules
quiz.explain: Fluency is built by producing language in real time; explicit rule knowledge alone does not automate speech.

quiz.prompt: An adult learner insists she can never sound native and so refuses to speak at all. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
quiz.answer: Being understood matters far more than accent does
choices: Being understood matters far more than accent does
Listening more will fix the accent without speaking
Accent fades by itself once vocabulary is large enough
Adults reach a native accent as easily as children do
quiz.explain: Intelligibility, not native-like accent, is the realistic and useful goal, and silence blocks the practice that builds it. Accent does not improve from input alone or from vocabulary growth, and late learners rarely reach a native accent at all — which is why it is the wrong bar to set.

quiz.prompt: A learner keeps a notebook of single words with English translations and finds them hard to use in speech. Suggest a better way to record vocabulary and explain why it works.
quiz.answer: Record each word inside a short example sentence from something you actually read or heard, because that stores the grammar, the collocations and the situation along with the word, so it comes back ready to use rather than as an isolated label.
quiz.explain: Words live in contexts; storing the context stores the information needed to deploy the word correctly.

lesson_media.alt: A daily learning loop connects comprehensible input, noticing a useful phrase, retrieving it from memory, using it in conversation and receiving corrective feedback.
lesson_media.caption: Frequent retrieval and meaningful use strengthen access to a second language. Feedback updates a learner's hypothesis, while spaced return is more useful than one long exposure.

nodes.title: Linguistics
nodes.goal: Syntax, semantics, phonology — formally.

quiz.prompt: The sentence "Colorless green ideas sleep furiously," coined by Chomsky, is famous because it is:
quiz.answer: Syntactically well-formed but semantically nonsensical
quiz.explain: The sentence obeys English syntax yet violates semantic sense, which is how Chomsky showed the two systems are independent. Readers can of course impose a metaphorical reading — that ingenuity is a fact about readers, not evidence that the sentence means anything on its own.
choices: Syntactically well-formed but semantically nonsensical
Ungrammatical, which is what makes it uninterpretable
Ill-formed in syntax yet perfectly interpretable as written
Readable as metaphor, so sense and syntax never come apart

quiz.prompt: "Visiting relatives can be tiring" is structurally ambiguous: one string of words corresponds to two different syntactic structures. Which sentence below is ambiguous for the same reason, rather than because a single word has two senses?
quiz.answer: They saw the guard with binoculars
quiz.explain: Both readings of "visiting relatives" come from one word string with two structures, and "with binoculars" likewise attaches either to "saw" or to "the guard". The other three turn on a single word — bat, figure, plant — carrying two senses, which is lexical ambiguity.
choices: They saw the guard with binoculars
The bat in the shed had not moved for days
She could not make out the figure in the dark
The plant will close at the end of the summer

quiz.prompt: In English, aspiration is allophonic: a voiceless stop is aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable ([pʰɪn] "pin") but plain after [s] ([spɪn] "spin"). Predict how an English speaker will say the invented words "pleeny" and "spleeny".
quiz.answer: Aspirated [pʰ] in "pleeny", plain [p] in "spleeny"
quiz.explain: Allophonic rules are productive: they apply to anything a speaker utters, invented words included. Aspiration is suppressed after [s], so "spleeny" takes plain [p] and "pleeny" takes [pʰ] — the same alternation as spin beside pin.
choices: Aspirated [pʰ] in "pleeny", plain [p] in "spleeny"
Aspirated [pʰ] in both, since English has one p sound
Plain [p] in "pleeny", aspirated in "spleeny"
Plain [p] in both, the rule holding only of real words

quiz.prompt: English speakers pluralise "cat" as [kæts] but "dog" as [dɒgz], and do the same to invented words they have never heard. State the rule that predicts which ending appears, and name the phonological process behind it.
quiz.answer: The plural suffix surfaces as [s] after a voiceless consonant and [z] after a voiced one: the suffix takes on the voicing of the sound immediately before it, which is assimilation.
quiz.explain: One underlying morpheme, three predictable surface forms — [s], [z] and [ɪz] — selected by the preceding segment. Regular alternation of this kind is why phonology is stated as rules rather than lists.

quiz.prompt: In "The student from Prague solved the puzzle," the string "the student from Prague" can be replaced by "she" and can be fronted as "It was the student from Prague who solved the puzzle," while the string "from Prague solved" can do neither. These facts are evidence that:
quiz.answer: "the student from Prague" forms one constituent
choices: "the student from Prague" forms one constituent
"from Prague solved" forms a constituent of its own
pronouns can substitute for just about any string of words
constituency is settled by meaning, not by tests
quiz.explain: Substitution and clefting are constituency tests: only a genuine syntactic unit passes them. Strings that merely sit next to each other, like "from Prague solved", fail both — and it is the tests, not intuitions about meaning, that decide.

quiz.prompt: A says "Some of the students passed." B infers "So not all of them did." A can continue "in fact all of them did" without contradicting herself. B's inference is therefore:
quiz.answer: A cancellable implicature
choices: A cancellable implicature
An entailment of the word "some"
A presupposition triggered by "the"
Vagueness about how many "some" covers
quiz.explain: An entailment cannot be cancelled without contradiction; a scalar implicature can, which is precisely the test. "Some" is logically compatible with "all", so the exclusion is pragmatic rather than semantic — and it is an exclusion, not mere haziness about number.

quiz.prompt: A student argues that English [ŋ] (as in 'sing') and [n] must be variants of one sound, since [ŋ] cannot start a word. A classmate disagrees. Which piece of evidence settles the dispute?
quiz.answer: A word pair differing in that sound alone but in meaning
choices: A word pair differing in that sound alone but in meaning
The restriction on where in the word each sound may occur
The fact that the two sounds are made at different places
Speakers' impression that the two sounds are similar
quiz.explain: Contrast, not distribution, defines a phoneme: a minimal pair such as sin/sing shows the two sounds distinguish words, so they are separate phonemes despite the positional restriction on [ŋ].

quiz.prompt: A logician glosses 'Every child climbed a tree' as one tree that the children shared; a friend insists each child had a different tree. Diagnose the disagreement.
quiz.answer: Both scope orders are available, so both readings exist
choices: Both scope orders are available, so both readings exist
The sentence is vague, and context merely fills in a single meaning
They disagree about the world described, not about the sentence
The plural subject forces the reading with separate trees
quiz.explain: This is scope ambiguity: the universal and the indefinite can each take wide scope, giving a shared-tree reading and a tree-per-child reading from one string of words.

quiz.prompt: An English speaker judges 'blick' to be a possible word that happens not to exist, but 'bnick' to be impossible. Name the kind of knowledge behind this judgement and state the constraint it applies.
quiz.answer: It reflects phonotactic knowledge: English permits /bl/ as a syllable onset but not /bn/, so 'blick' is an accidental gap in the lexicon while 'bnick' is a systematic gap ruled out by the grammar of possible sound sequences.
quiz.explain: Speakers know rules over sound sequences, not just a list of words, which is why they can sort non-words into possible and impossible ones.

quiz.prompt: Children learning English produce 'Is the boy who is crying happy?' and do not produce 'Is the boy who crying is happy?', even though the second follows a simpler recipe. Predict what this shows about the question rule.
quiz.answer: It targets the main clause's auxiliary, found by structure
choices: It targets the main clause's auxiliary, found by structure
It moves whichever auxiliary comes first in the string of words
It waits until children can handle relative clauses
It is memorised sentence by sentence from adult speech
quiz.explain: Question formation is structure-dependent: it picks the auxiliary of the main clause, so the auxiliary inside the relative clause is skipped even though it comes earlier in the string.

lesson_media.alt: Four branches analyze Those dogs bark as a sound phrase, plural-agreement morphology, the syntax noun phrase plus verb phrase, and a compositional proposition.
lesson_media.caption: Formal analysis separates but connects phonological form, morphosyntactic features, constituent structure, and semantic composition. Evidence determines which representation is appropriate.

nodes.title: Literary Theory
nodes.goal: Formalism to post-structuralism: ways of reading.

quiz.prompt: New Criticism holds that a poem's meaning is carried by its language and internal structure, not by the author's biography or the reader's feelings. Two students disagree about the tone of a line. Which evidence would a New Critic accept as settling it?
quiz.answer: The imagery patterned across the rest of the poem
quiz.explain: Formalism and New Criticism locate meaning in the text's formal features. The three rejected options are the three rival schools in miniature — biographical, reader-response and historicist — and each imports evidence from outside the poem.
choices: The imagery patterned across the rest of the poem
A letter in which the poet describes his mood that winter
A survey of how present-day readers report feeling
The politics of the country in the year it was written

quiz.prompt: Structuralism analyzes literature by treating meaning as arising from:
quiz.answer: Systems of differences and relations, as in linguistics
quiz.explain: Drawing on Saussurean linguistics, structuralism holds that meaning emerges from relations and differences within a system of signs, not from words naming things, from an author's feelings, or from a readership's class.
choices: Systems of differences and relations, as in linguistics
The author's private emotions at the very moment of writing
A one-to-one match between each word and the thing it names
The economic class of the book's intended readership

quiz.prompt: Reader-response theory differs from formalism chiefly in that it locates a text's meaning primarily in:
quiz.answer: The reader's active process of interpretation
quiz.explain: Reader-response theory holds that meaning is produced in the transaction between text and reader — not fixed in the words alone as formalists claim, nor settled by intention or historical setting.
choices: The reader's active process of interpretation
The historical events surrounding first publication
The author's stated intention in writing it
The fixed words printed on the page alone

quiz.prompt: Wimsatt and Beardsley called it a fallacy to settle a poem's meaning by asking what the poet says they meant. Explain their objection and one cost of accepting it.
quiz.answer: This is the intentional fallacy: the poem's meaning is public property made by its words, while the author's private intention is neither reliably available nor binding on the text; the cost is that biography, letters and stated purpose lose their evidential force even where they would genuinely illuminate the poem.
quiz.explain: The argument is that a poem, once published, is a public linguistic object, and that appeals to intention import evidence from outside it. The price is a criticism that has to discard some of what we know.

quiz.prompt: Postcolonial criticism attends to the empire a metropolitan novel keeps offstage: the colonial money, places and people its plot requires but never examines. Applied to Mansfield Park, whose Sir Thomas Bertram owns an estate in Antigua, which question does the method put first?
quiz.answer: Where the plantation income comes from, and at what cost
choices: Where the plantation income comes from, and at what cost
Whether Fanny Price's speech is convincingly rendered throughout
How the novel's chapter divisions shape its pacing
What Austen's letters say she intended
quiz.explain: Postcolonial criticism reads the empire that the plot needs but will not look at. The other three questions belong to character criticism, formal analysis and biography — all legitimate, none of them this method.

quiz.prompt: Deconstruction works from inside a text, showing that an opposition the text depends on will not hold in its own terms. A critic takes an essay that defends "natural" childhood against "artificial" screens. Which move is the deconstructive one?
quiz.answer: Showing its "natural" childhood already runs on books and clocks
choices: Showing its "natural" childhood already runs on books and clocks
Showing its claims about childhood are contradicted by recent research
Showing its author holds shares in a publisher of children's books
Showing its natural/artificial binary was common in Romantic writing
quiz.explain: Deconstruction turns the text's own terms against it, rather than refuting it from outside. Empirical refutation, ideological unmasking and tracing a binary to its historical source are three other real critical moves — and none of them shows the opposition collapsing internally.

quiz.prompt: Wimsatt and Beardsley's affective fallacy is the error of settling a poem's value by the response it produces in readers. Which defence of a poem commits it?
quiz.answer: The audience wept at the reading, so the ending is earned
choices: The audience wept at the reading, so the ending is earned
The poet wrote it the week after his brother's death
Its final stanza reverses the syntax of its first
Its plain diction was unusual for the year it appeared
quiz.explain: The affective fallacy is the mirror image of the intentional fallacy: the first confuses the poem with what readers feel, the second with what the author meant. Formal and historical evidence, by contrast, are exactly what these critics would allow.

quiz.prompt: Marxist criticism reads literary form as bound up with the economic relations a work depends on, especially the ones it declines to represent. Applied to a novel set in a serene country house, which observation belongs to that method?
quiz.answer: The calm rests on rents and enclosures the book never shows
choices: The calm rests on rents and enclosures the book never shows
The house recurs as a symbol of the heroine's inner peace
The author's own childhood home resembled the house
The rooms are described in unusually long, unbroken sentences
quiz.explain: Marxist criticism asks what economic arrangement a literary form takes for granted, and what it must keep offstage to seem natural. Symbol-hunting, biography and sentence-length belong to other methods entirely.

quiz.prompt: A student sums up 'the death of the author' as meaning that biography is off limits and that any reading is as good as any other. Correct both halves of that summary.
quiz.answer: Barthes displaces the author as the guarantor of meaning, making the reader the site where a text's threads converge; that does not forbid using biography as evidence, and it does not license anything at all, since readings are still answerable to the language of the text.
quiz.explain: Removing the author as final arbiter is a claim about where meaning is made, not a licence for unconstrained interpretation.

quiz.prompt: For Bakhtin, heteroglossia is the novel's capacity to hold many socially marked languages in tension without subordinating them to one authoritative voice. Which revision would most reduce a novel's heteroglossia?
quiz.answer: Giving lawyer, merchant and preacher one shared narrating idiom
choices: Giving lawyer, merchant and preacher one shared narrating idiom
Letting the merchant answer the preacher at considerably greater length
Moving one long argument from summary into direct speech
Adding a fourth speaker with an idiom of her own
quiz.explain: Heteroglossia lives in the difference between socially marked languages, so flattening them into one idiom is what destroys it. Lengthening a speech, dramatising an argument or adding a voice all leave the contest of languages intact or enlarge it.

lesson_media.alt: Four critical approaches ask different questions of the same unnamed text: formal pattern, historical conditions, reader response and instability in its oppositions.
lesson_media.caption: A critical lens foregrounds particular evidence and questions; it is not a machine that guarantees one answer. Interpretations remain accountable to the text and their stated assumptions.

nodes.title: Creative Writing
nodes.goal: Write fiction or poetry seriously; revise ruthlessly.

quiz.prompt: The writing maxim "Show, don't tell" advises a writer to:
quiz.answer: Reveal emotion through action rather than naming it
quiz.explain: "Show, don't tell" urges rendering a feeling through observable detail (a trembling hand) rather than flatly asserting it ("she was nervous"). It is not a licence to describe more: piled-up detail and piled-up adjectives are their own kind of telling.
choices: Reveal emotion through action rather than naming it
Describe every object in the room in unhurried detail
State each character's feelings in a plain summary line
Use as many vivid adjectives as you possibly can

quiz.prompt: Which revision best replaces the flat sentence "She was very sad" by showing rather than telling?
quiz.answer: She read his note twice, folded it, and stared at nothing.
quiz.explain: Concrete, observable action lets the reader infer the grief, which is the essence of showing rather than telling.
choices: She read his note twice, folded it, and stared at nothing.
She felt a great and overwhelming sadness rising inside her.
She was extremely, deeply, terribly sad about all of it.
Sadness was the emotion she quietly experienced at the time.

quiz.prompt: A workshop leader tells a writer to revise "ruthlessly". Which change best fits what she means?
quiz.answer: Cutting a favourite paragraph that no longer serves the story
quiz.explain: Ruthless revision — "kill your darlings" — means cutting what does not earn its place, including the parts you like best. Proofreading, word-polishing and explaining more are all things writers do to a draft instead of revising it.
choices: Cutting a favourite paragraph that no longer serves the story
Replacing plain words with more striking ones throughout
Fixing the spelling and punctuation across the whole draft
Adding a scene that explains the ending more clearly

quiz.prompt: A first draft ends with a character explaining the story's meaning aloud to a friend on the last page. Say why editors distrust endings like this and what to do instead.
quiz.answer: It tells the reader what to think and dissolves the tension the scene has built; better to trust the reader and let the closing action or image carry the meaning.
quiz.explain: An ending that explains itself takes the discovery away from the reader. The image or gesture that ends a strong story means more precisely because nobody paraphrases it.

quiz.prompt: Free indirect discourse folds a character's own idiom and judgement into third-person narration, with no quotation marks and no "she thought" tag. Which sentence uses it?
quiz.answer: She would not cry. Crying was for people with somewhere to go.
choices: She would not cry. Crying was for people with somewhere to go.
"Crying," she said, "is for people with somewhere to go."
She thought that crying was for people with somewhere to go.
The narrator observed that she did not permit herself to cry.
quiz.explain: The voice belongs to two people at once: the grammar is the narrator's, the judgement is hers. Quoted speech, a reporting tag and a narrator's own comment each keep the two voices safely apart.

quiz.prompt: A workshop marks this as the weakest line in a story: "Tom felt an indescribable sadness that words could not capture." What is the strongest objection to it?
quiz.answer: It names a feeling and then declines to render it
choices: It names a feeling and then declines to render it
It uses "felt", a filter verb that weakens the prose
It uses the past tense where the present would be livelier
It contains an adverb, and fiction ought to avoid them
quiz.explain: The sentence asserts an emotion and then excuses itself from showing it, which leaves the reader nothing to feel. Trimming "felt" would tidy the surface; the ban on adverbs and the preference for the present tense are workshop folklore, and there is no adverb here anyway.

quiz.prompt: A story told in the first person past tense contains the line 'Unknown to me, the sheriff was already loading his rifle.' A workshop objects. Diagnose the fault.
quiz.answer: The narrator reports what she could not have known
choices: The narrator reports what she could not have known
The past tense drains the moment of its suspense
The sentence relies on a passive construction
The detail arrives too early in the story
quiz.explain: A first-person narrator can only report what she perceives, learns or infers; slipping into omniscience breaks the contract the point of view has set up. The tense is fine, the verb is active, and the timing is not the problem.

quiz.prompt: Which revision most improves the flat line 'The room was messy, and it made her feel out of control'?
quiz.answer: Three cereal bowls crusted on the sill. She counted them twice.
choices: Three cereal bowls crusted on the sill. She counted them twice.
The room, messy beyond description, mirrored her turmoil.
She felt out of control, because the room around her was so messy.
The room was extremely messy, and chaos rose in her like a tide.
quiz.explain: The strong revision replaces the abstraction with concrete detail and an action that lets the reader infer the feeling. The other three keep telling — one of them twice over, once in a simile.

quiz.prompt: An editor cuts the adverbs from 'He said angrily, slamming the door violently.' Predict the reasoning behind the cut.
quiz.answer: The verbs already carry the force the adverbs restate
choices: The verbs already carry the force the adverbs restate
Two modifiers in one sentence break a grammatical rule
Adverbs belong in dialogue rather than in narration
The anger needs to be stated even more plainly
quiz.explain: "Slamming" is already violent and the slam already reads as anger; the adverbs add nothing and dilute verbs that were doing the work. No grammatical rule is broken, and no rule confines adverbs to dialogue.

quiz.prompt: A draft spends its first two pages on a character's childhood before anything happens in the present. Name the structural problem and give the standard fix.
quiz.answer: The story starts too early, front-loading backstory before the reader has any reason to care; cut into the scene where the trouble begins and release the childhood material later, in small pieces, where it earns its place.
quiz.explain: Readers accept exposition once they are invested in a present-tense problem, so late entry into the scene and dripped-in history usually beats a chronological opening.

lesson_media.alt: A revision cycle turns The storm was bad into Rain hammered the tin roof by identifying vague language, selecting sensory evidence and checking whether the new verb fits the scene.
lesson_media.caption: Revision is a sequence of decisions, not mere polishing. A writer diagnoses what the draft fails to convey, changes specific language, then rereads for accuracy, rhythm, and consequence.

nodes.title: History of English
nodes.goal: Beowulf to blogs: a thousand years of change.

quiz.prompt: "Beowulf" was composed in the earliest recorded stage of English, which is largely unintelligible to modern readers without study. This stage is called:
quiz.answer: Old English
quiz.explain: Old English (c. 450–1150), the language of Beowulf, differs so greatly from today's English in vocabulary and grammar that it must be studied like a foreign language.
choices: Old English
Proto-Indo-European
Early Modern English
Middle English

quiz.prompt: The Norman Conquest of 1066 most profoundly affected English by:
quiz.answer: Bringing in French words for law, government and food
quiz.explain: After 1066 Norman French became the language of the ruling class, and English took thousands of French words. The grammar stayed Germanic, the Latin alphabet had been used for English since the seventh century, and English writing thinned for about two centuries rather than stopping for five.
choices: Bringing in French words for law, government and food
Replacing English grammar with the grammar of Norman French
Bringing the Latin alphabet to England for the first time
Ending the writing of English until the sixteenth century

quiz.prompt: The pairing of the Germanic word "cow" (the live animal, tended by English-speaking farmers) with the French-derived "beef" (the meat, served to Norman lords) is often cited as evidence of:
quiz.answer: Social layering that followed the Norman Conquest
quiz.explain: The animal/meat word pairs (cow/beef, pig/pork) reflect Anglo-Saxon farmers and French-speaking nobility, a social division dating from the Norman Conquest.
choices: Borrowing from Old Norse during the Viking age
Social layering that followed the Norman Conquest
The Great Vowel Shift in later English pronunciation
A deliberate spelling reform of the early 1800s

quiz.prompt: Old English "stān" and "bāt" are today's "stone" and "boat", and Old English "hūs" was pronounced with the vowel of modern "goose" but is spelled "house". Using these, explain in a sentence or two why English spelling and pronunciation drifted so far apart.
quiz.answer: The spellings were fixed by printing and by scribal habit while the long vowels went on shifting, so the letters still record a pronunciation that English has since abandoned.
quiz.explain: Caxton's press froze written forms in the late fifteenth century, in the middle of the Great Vowel Shift. English spelling is therefore a photograph of a pronunciation that kept moving.

quiz.prompt: The Great Vowel Shift raised the English long vowels between roughly 1400 and 1700, the highest of them breaking into diphthongs, while printing froze many spellings partway through. Which fact about present-day English follows from that?
quiz.answer: Vowel letters record the older sound, as in "name" and "mice"
choices: Vowel letters record the older sound, as in "name" and "mice"
Consonants have gone silent in writing, as in "knight" and "gnaw"
Short vowel spellings stay unpredictable, as in "bread" and "friend"
French spellings sit beside English ones, as in "chef"
quiz.explain: "Name" was [naːmə] and "mice" was [miːs] when their spellings settled; the letters still record those vowels. The other three statements are true of English but caused by something else — consonant loss, an already-stable short-vowel system, and borrowing.

quiz.prompt: English took "they", "them" and "their" from Old Norse, displacing native forms that began with h-. Languages very rarely borrow pronouns. What does this particular borrowing suggest about Norse and English contact?
quiz.answer: Long, close contact between speakers of both
choices: Long, close contact between speakers of both
A written borrowing made by scholars from books
That Norse replaced English as the spoken language
A brief trading contact confined to the port towns
quiz.explain: Core grammatical words pass between languages only where communities live mixed together and speak both — as Danes and English did in the Danelaw. Trade borrows nouns, books borrow learned words, and outright replacement would have left Norse, not English, behind.

quiz.prompt: In Old English, 'Se hund biteþ þone mann' and 'Þone mann biteþ se hund' both mean the dog bites the man; in Modern English, swapping the two noun phrases reverses who bites whom. Diagnose the change.
quiz.answer: Case endings eroded, so word order marks the roles
choices: Case endings eroded, so word order marks the roles
English adopted its word order directly from Norman French
The verb shifted to a new position in the clause
Modern articles now assign the roles instead
quiz.explain: Old English marked subject and object with inflectional case, so order was free; as those endings levelled, English came to rely on fixed word order. French had a similar history but did not impose it, and English articles carry no case.

quiz.prompt: A writer choosing among 'kingly', 'royal' and 'regal' finds they feel plain, official and lofty in turn. Explain the pattern.
quiz.answer: Germanic, French and Latin sources at three levels of formality
choices: Germanic, French and Latin sources at three levels of formality
Three spellings that one Old English word gradually acquired
Regional variants preserved from three areas of England
Coinages made by Renaissance poets for metrical variety
quiz.explain: English's layered vocabulary gives many such triplets: the native word is plain, the French-derived word official, and the Latin-derived word learned or elevated.

quiz.prompt: A student wants to compare independent copies of Beowulf to see which readings are original. Give the number of medieval manuscripts of the poem that survive.
quiz.explain: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, damaged by fire in 1731 — so there are no rival copies against which to check its readings.

quiz.prompt: A blogger writes 'literally' where the sense is figurative, and a commenter calls it an illiterate error. Give the historical linguist's reply, citing a parallel from earlier English.
quiz.answer: Intensifiers routinely drift from literal to emphatic: 'very' descends from a word meaning 'truly', and 'really' and 'terribly' have travelled the same road, so 'literally' as an intensifier is ordinary semantic change rather than a failure of literacy.
quiz.explain: The complaint tradition regularly targets changes that have already happened many times over in the language's history.

lesson_media.alt: A timeline follows Old English cniht with pronounced initial consonants through Middle English knyght to present-day knight, where the k and gh are no longer pronounced.
lesson_media.caption: English changes in sound, spelling, meaning, and grammar at different rates. Knight preserves letters associated with earlier pronunciations; spelling is historical evidence, not a phonetic transcript.

nodes.title: The Ancient Canon
nodes.goal: Homer, Virgil, and the epics beneath Western literature.

quiz.prompt: Epic convention opens in medias res — in the middle of the action — and supplies the earlier events afterwards. Which opening follows the convention?
quiz.answer: A fleet is wrecked by a storm; the war it fled is told later
quiz.explain: In medias res means the poem starts inside the action and recovers what led there through narration later — as the Aeneid does with its storm and Aeneas's retelling of Troy. A chronological life, a prologue and a scene-setting preamble all begin at or before the beginning.
choices: A fleet is wrecked by a storm; the war it fled is told later
A poet describes his village before naming any character
A god sets out the whole plot before the action begins
A hero is born, and the poem follows him year by year

quiz.prompt: Virgil's "Aeneid" deliberately models itself on Homer and traces its hero Aeneas from Troy to Italy, casting him as ancestor of the Romans. Its evident purpose includes:
quiz.answer: Giving Rome a founding epic linked to the Trojan past
quiz.explain: The Aeneid was crafted as a national epic connecting Rome and Augustus to the prestige of the Homeric tradition. It is modelled on Homer rather than translated from him, it stops long before Romulus, and it was written some twelve centuries after the war it invokes.
choices: Giving Rome a founding epic linked to the Trojan past
Rendering Homer's two poems into Latin for Roman readers
Narrating Romulus's own founding of the city of Rome
Recording an eyewitness history of the Trojan War

quiz.prompt: The Iliad concentrates on a short span near the end of the Trojan War, centering on the consequences of one hero's rage. That hero is:
quiz.answer: Achilles
quiz.explain: The Iliad's opening word is "rage" (mēnis), the wrath of Achilles, whose anger drives the poem's action. Agamemnon provokes that anger, Patroclus's death redirects it, and Hector is its eventual victim — but none of them is the poem's announced subject.
choices: Agamemnon
Hector
Achilles
Patroclus

quiz.prompt: Homer's poems are full of fixed phrases such as "swift-footed Achilles" and "rosy-fingered Dawn", repeated wherever the metre allows. Explain what these formulas tell us about how the poems were made.
quiz.answer: They are metrical building blocks: a singer composing aloud in performance reached for a ready-made phrase that filled the end of the hexameter line, which shows the poems grew out of oral composition rather than being written sentence by sentence.
quiz.explain: Milman Parry showed that the epithets are distributed by metrical convenience, not by meaning — Achilles is swift-footed even when sitting down. That distribution is the fingerprint of oral composition.

quiz.prompt: An epic simile opens a whole second world — often a peaceful, domestic one — inside the poem's violence, and sustains it well past the point of comparison. Which passage is one?
quiz.answer: Six lines on a wheelwright felling a poplar, then the warrior drops
choices: Six lines on a wheelwright felling a poplar, then the warrior drops
A single line calling the warrior a lion loose among the sheep
The phrase "swift-footed Achilles", used wherever the metre allows
A long list of the ships and captains who sailed from each town
quiz.explain: What makes the epic simile epic is its length and its second world, sustained until the reader almost forgets the battle. A one-line comparison is an ordinary simile, a fixed descriptive tag is an epithet, and a list of ships is a catalogue.

quiz.prompt: Aristotle's peripeteia is a reversal in which an action produces the opposite of its intended effect. Which turn in a plot is one?
quiz.answer: A messenger brings news meant to comfort, and it damns the hearer
choices: A messenger brings news meant to comfort, and it damns the hearer
A ruler's early misjudgement quietly sets the whole disaster going
A hero learns at last that the beggar was his own father
A god descends at the end and settles the quarrel
quiz.explain: Aristotle takes the Corinthian messenger in Oedipus as his model of peripeteia. Recognition is anagnorisis, the founding error is hamartia, and a god arriving to settle things is the deus ex machina Aristotle disliked.

quiz.prompt: Aeneas abandons Dido at the gods' command, and Virgil goes on calling him 'pius'. A reader finds the epithet callous. What value is the poem asserting?
quiz.answer: Duty to fate and the future city outweighs private feeling
choices: Duty to fate and the future city outweighs private feeling
The poem invites the reader to condemn its hero as a villain
His attachment to Dido was a pretence from the beginning
The gods are punishing him for lingering in Carthage
quiz.explain: "Pietas" names duty to gods, family and community; the Dido episode makes the cost of that duty painfully visible without withdrawing the epithet.

quiz.prompt: Odysseus spends four books of the Odyssey telling the Phaeacians about the Cyclops and the underworld, events long past by the time he speaks. Describe what the poem is doing here.
quiz.answer: It embeds a first-person report inside the poet's own narrative
choices: It embeds a first-person report inside the poet's own narrative
It flashes back in the singer's own voice to earlier events
It reports a prophecy that a god has delivered to the hero
It preserves a digression added by a much later editor
quiz.explain: The adventures reach us through Odysseus as narrator, a story within the story — which is also why their truth depends on a famously persuasive speaker.

quiz.prompt: The Iliad closes not with the fall of Troy but with Priam ransoming Hector's body from Achilles. Explain what that choice of ending tells us about the poem's subject.
quiz.answer: The poem announces the wrath of Achilles as its subject, not the war's outcome, so it ends when that wrath is released in the shared grief of the killer and the victim's father; its subject is mortality, honour and pity rather than victory.
quiz.explain: Reading the ending back onto the proem shows the Iliad is a poem about a quarrel and its human cost, framed by a war it never narrates to its conclusion.

quiz.prompt: Suppose a modern play shows a competent, decent surgeon whose single misjudgement destroys his family. Aristotle would locate the tragic effect in:
quiz.answer: hamartia, an error by a man neither good nor wicked
choices: hamartia, an error by a man neither good nor wicked
anagnorisis, the recognition scene late in the action
catharsis, the purging that the spectacle produces
hubris, arrogance that the gods move to punish
quiz.explain: Aristotle's tragic hero falls through hamartia — a mistake or misjudgement — precisely because a wholly wicked or wholly blameless downfall would not move us to pity and fear. Recognition and catharsis are effects of the plot, not its cause, and nothing here suggests arrogance.

lesson_media.alt: A chain links Homeric epic conventions to Virgil's selective Roman adaptation and then to later readers who translate, imitate, contest and reinterpret both traditions.
lesson_media.caption: Classical reception is active transformation. The Aeneid draws on Homeric forms while redirecting them toward Roman history; later works inherit choices, not an unchanged universal template.

nodes.title: Comparative Literature
nodes.goal: Read across languages and traditions systematically.

quiz.prompt: Translation studies holds that no choice of word is neutral, since connotations rarely cross languages intact. A French novel's "terroir" is rendered once as "soil", once as "local character", and once left untranslated. What does the case best illustrate?
quiz.answer: Each rendering keeps part of the sense and gives up the rest
quiz.explain: Translation studies examines what each choice buys and what it costs. Treating one option as simply right, or the word as simply untranslatable, both dodge the question of which part of the meaning a given context needs.
choices: Each rendering keeps part of the sense and gives up the rest
The most literal rendering must be the most faithful of the three
Two of the three are simply errors that a reviser ought to correct
The word has no meaning that English is able to express

quiz.prompt: Comparative literature studies texts across languages, national traditions and disciplines. A student proposes four projects. Which one falls outside the field as so defined?
quiz.answer: Tracing one image through three novels by a single English writer
quiz.explain: Comparative literature crosses a boundary of language, nation or medium. A single author in a single language crosses none of them, however careful the reading — that is national literary study, and a perfectly good thing to do under another name.
choices: Tracing one image through three novels by a single English writer
Setting a Caribbean novel against the two films made from it
Reading Japanese and German ghost tales beside one another
Comparing a Persian romance with its later French analogue

quiz.prompt: Foreignization keeps a source text's strangeness in view; domestication smooths it into the target culture. A translator handles a Japanese meal scene. Which choice is the domesticating one?
quiz.answer: Turning "onigiri" into "sandwiches" for the English reader
quiz.explain: Domestication replaces the foreign item with a familiar one, so the reader never meets the difference. The other three keep the word and vary only how much help they give, which is foreignization at three levels of hospitality.
choices: Turning "onigiri" into "sandwiches" for the English reader
Printing "onigiri (rice balls)" at its first appearance only
Keeping "onigiri" and letting the scene itself explain it
Keeping "onigiri" and adding a note at the foot of the page

quiz.prompt: A prize jury reads every submission in English translation and gives the award to a novel it praises for its "crystalline prose". Explain what that praise cannot safely be credited to, and why.
quiz.answer: The prose the jury read is the translator's: sentence rhythm, diction and clarity are choices made in English, so the praise cannot safely be credited to the original author's style without reading the source text.
quiz.explain: Style is the most language-bound thing a novel has. Judging it through translation is judging a collaboration, which is why serious prizes now name the translator alongside the author.

quiz.prompt: Compensation recreates in the target language an effect the source produced by means the target lacks, trading fidelity of image for fidelity of function. Which decision is compensation?
quiz.answer: Inventing an English pun where the original punned on a character
choices: Inventing an English pun where the original punned on a character
Rendering the punning phrase in its plainest literal sense
Cutting the sentence, since the pun cannot be carried over
Adding a footnote explaining the pun in the original
quiz.explain: Compensation reproduces what the original did to its reader by means the target language does have. A footnote reports the effect, a literal rendering loses it, and cutting removes the problem along with the passage.

quiz.prompt: Two novels written in the same decade, one in Bengali and one in Spanish, share a plot of a village swallowed by a river and a narrator who addresses the dead. Neither author read the other's language and no translation existed. A comparatist should treat the resemblance as:
quiz.answer: an analogy, not a case of direct influence
choices: an analogy, not a case of direct influence
proof that one text was copied from the other
a coincidence with nothing to say to criticism
evidence that both descend from one lost original
quiz.explain: Comparative literature distinguishes influence, which needs a demonstrable route of transmission, from analogy, where similar conditions produce similar forms independently — and analogies are often the more interesting finding.
